speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure I shall have the unanimous approval of all present in extending to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) congratulations upon his recovery and a most cordial welcome in his return to the house. During his absence we watched with some concern the occasional reports on his progress. While I cannot always speak with the unanimous support of hon. members in the house, I am sure that on this occasion I do so when I say we are glad to see him back. We trust he has fully recovered, and we wish for him only the best of health and strength in the strenuous days ahead.

subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) has said I am sure he has the unanimous support of all hon. members. We join with all others in the house in expressing our pleasure at seeing the Prime Minister back, and we express the hope that his good health may long continue.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I am sure I represent the views of all those in this group when I join with the other two hon. members who have spoken to welcome the Prime Minister back to the house after his illness, and to say to him we are happy he has weathered the storm and is back looking as well as he does. Let me hope the Prime Minister will not be able to say, as Sir John A. Macdonald once said, "Those leaders of the opposition, when they speak, always do make me sick".

subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the
gracious speeches which have been made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) and the leader of the Social Credit group (Mr. Low). On behalf of the rank and file of the Liberal party I am delighted to welcome the Prime Minister to the house. We were told that he was not well-but he looks so well. Perhaps he just wanted to meditate about public policies. But he had us all worried about him. It is a source of satisfaction now to see him looking so hale and hearty, and especially to see him with his good smile. The Prime Minister, when he smiles, is not at
The Prime Minister

all the same man as when he frowns. I prefer him when he is smiling, and I offer him our very best wishes.

subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS
speechtext: What group are you speaking for?

subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS
speechtext:
I am speaking for all men of good will, of whom there must be quite a number in this chamber. Of course the Prime Minister may at times leave the house when he feels like it. I can tell him however that the discussions in the house and the atmosphere of it are quite different from what they are when he is outside the country. When he is within the country the only thing we have to report to him is progress.
Many members of parliament have spoken, and all have made good speeches, worthy of their constituencies. They have tried to make things as smooth as possible for the Prime Minister, so that he would have no trouble when he came back. Now he is here with us and again I extend to him our best wishes. If my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, had not spoken so well, I would have extended wishes also on his behalf.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I need
scarcely say how deeply grateful I am to my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, to the leaders of other parties and to the hon. member for Temiscouata for the very kind remarks they have just made. May I say to the entire membership of the house how deeply I appreciate the kindly manner in which hon. members have received my return to my accustomed seat in this chamber. I
I should like also to say how very much I appreciated the kind inquiries and messages which throughout my absence came from hon. members to Laurier House. I assure Your Honour, it has been a matter of deep regret to me to have been unavoidably absent during the past three weeks. I certainly shall do all within my power from now on not to have a repetition of anything of the kind I have recently experienced. May I say that I realize at this moment, perhaps as I never have done before, what it means to be able in health and strength to participate in the proceedings of the House of Commons, and to enjoy the companionship of one's fellow members in parliament.
I do thank hon. members most warmly for the kind welcome which they have just given to me. I shall do my best to be on hand right along, but if I should find it desirable to take things a little easy for a short time I know I may count on the understanding of hon. members of the house.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: WARTIME HOUSING-HAMILTON AND WENTWORTH COUNTY
speechtext:
1.	No.
2.	No. However, general policy of the sale of Wartime Housing houses to tenants has
been introduced. It is contingent, however, in most cases, on the municipality concerned being prepared to negotiate a new agreement permitting this sale. When this renegotiation is completed and the land surveyed, tenants are given the opportunity of purchasing under conditions outlined hereunder, or, alternatively, they may remain as tenants. The conditions of sale are:
(a)	Sale is effected only to tenants.
(b)	Minimum down payment of fifteen per cent and monthly minimum payments at the normal rate they now pay in the form of rent. This will include insurance, taxes, interest and capital.
(c)	The tenant cannot acquire title of the property for a period of five years. The object of this restriction is to prevent resale and speculation.
(d)	On completion of the agreement of sale the normal tax rate of the municipality becomes applicable.
(e)	Every endeavour is made to ensure fair appraisal values when houses are sold to tenants.
3.	During the war years, houses built by Wartime Housing Limited were tenanted by munitions workers, some of whom were veterans. Mr. ST. LAURENT:
1.	The government has not appointed an ambassador to India; a high commissioner to India has, however, been appointed.
2.	J. D. Kearney, K.C.; recommended by the government of Canada; salary $10,000; allowances not yet decided.
3.	Tentative arrangements are being made to send a staff of five. Their total salary would be $13,200. Allowances for this staff have not yet been decided.
4.	No provisional government was set up in India last December. In August, 1946, the Viceroy of India, with the approval of the United Kingdom government, invited Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, president of the Indian political organization known as the All-India Congress, to make proposals for the immediate formation of an interim government. Pandit Nehru thereupon proposed a list of names for inclusion in the interim government. These were approved by His Majesty the King and made public on August 24. They included representatives of the congress party, the scheduled castes, the Sikhs, the Christians, the Parsees, and the Moslems, but not of the principal Moslem political party known as the Moslem League. This interim government was sworn in and took office on September 2, 1946. On October 26 it was reorganized to include five members of the Moslem League. No question of non-recognition has arisen, The interim government is recognized by the governments of all other countries, including the government of Canada.
5.	No dominion has an embassy in India. Australia has a high commissioner's office in India.

1.	Is the government aware that the new so-called provisional government constitutional meeting at Delhi, India, was held without the Moslems being represented?

3.	Has the government any immigration, commercial or other agents in India? If so, how many; at w'hat cost and where are they located.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:
1.	The government is not aware of any so-called provisional government constitutional meeting at Delhi, India.
A constituent assembly commenced its meetings on December 9, 1946. It is composed of members elected by the legislative assemblies of the Indian provinces, and is charged with the duty of drawing up a constitution for India, For the purpose of electing representatives to the constituent assembly, each legislative assembly was divided into three sections, composed respectively of Moslem representatives, Sikh representatives and representatives of all other communities. Each of these sections in each assembly elected its own representatives to the	constituent
assembly, thus enabling all the principal Indian communities to be represented.
The representatives who belong to the principal Moslem political organization, the Moslem League, have not, up to the present, exercised their right to attend the meetings of the constituent assembly.
2.	No information.
3. The government has no immigration agents in India.
In so far as the Department of Trade and Commerce is concerned, we do maintain a trade commissioner office in Bombay, India. The total expenditure for the fiscal year 194546 was $17,998.

maintopic: WITHDRAWAL OF OCCUPATIONAL FORCES FROM EUROPE
WITHDRAWAL OF OCCUPATIONAL FORCES FROM EUROPE
speechtext: For a copy of all correspondence, letters, telegrams, and other documents exchanged between the government of Canada, and the government of Great Britain, or any members or officials thereof relative to the withdrawal of the Canadian occupational forces from Europe.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: WITHDRAWAL OF OCCUPATIONAL FORCES FROM EUROPE
speechtext:
This motion is in similar terms to that which, was made by the hon. member for Nanaimo during the last session. It came up for consideration on April
8.	At the time, I felt obliged to point out that correspondence of the kind was, according to long-standing precedent, privileged. I asked the hon. member not to press for it, because it would not be possible to meet his wishes. To the motion as it stands on today's order paper I would have to make a similar reply.
Correspondence betiveen governments if of a secret or confidential nature, is not normally made public unless the consent of all the governments concerned has first been asked and obtained. Apart from this, it is the practice for the governments of the nations of the British commonwealth to communicate with one another freely and frankly on all questions of common concern. Such communications are not in general intended to be made public. To create a precedent under which communications of this character were made public in little more than a year after they were written, might inhibit in future full and frank communications between the governments of nations of the British, commonwealth. It is therefore the view of the Canadian government that it would not be in the public interest to table, at the present time, the correspondence between the Canadian and the United Kingdom governments on the withdrawal of Canadian occupational forces from Europe.
Having said this much, I hasten to add that in bringing forward this motion a year ago, the hon. member stated in reply to what I had then said:
If the Prime Minister is unable to produce all the papers, perhaps he could produce sufficient to clear up the matter, or he may be prepared to make a statement with regard to the reasons behind the withdrawal of this force.
To this I replied that I had no doubt the matter would come up when the minister of defence would be dealing w'ith his estimates or at some other appropriate moment; that I knew the minister would be only too ready to make a statement at that time.
I was absent in the United Kingdom when the defence estimates were being discussed in the house and unable, therefore, to say just how far statements made by the minister at the time may have covered the matter to the satisfaction of my hon. friend.
May I say that the request of the hon. member, in asking, if the Prime Minister was unable to produce all the papers, perhaps he could produce sufficient to clear up the matter, or might be prepared to make a statement with regard to the reasons behind the withdrawal of this force, seems to me a wholly reasonable one, and had) I been in the house when the defence estimates were before the house a year ago, I wouldi have been prepared to make the statement requested. The government has every reason for desiring that the facts be known and understood.
In the expectation that my hon. friend would be prepared to take the same attitude today as he did a year ago, I have endeavoured to meet his wishes by preparing a statement with regard to the reasons behind the withdrawal of the force. The statement is based on the communications exchanged between our government and the government of the United Kingdom and will, I believe, without creating a precedent which might inhibit in future full and frank communications between the governments of nations of the British commonwealth, meet in full the request for the reasons relative to the withdrawal of the Canadian army occupational forces from Germany.
The question of the provision of Canadian forces for occupational duty in Germany, after the defeat of Germany had been achieved, was one which was given very careful consideration over a considerable period of time. As a matter of fact, the matter was referred to in several telegrams between the governments of the United Kingdom and Canada over a period of a year and a half prior to January, 1945. It was also discussed with Mr. Churchill and the United Kingdom chiefs of staff on the occasion of the Quebec conference in September, 1944. There were further consultations through service channels.
On January 9, 1945, the United Kingdom government was informed that our government had decided to provide, for a period yet to be determined:, one army occupational group of approximately 25,000 all ranks for duty within the British zone of occupation in Germany and eleven R.C.A.F. squadrons to be stationed partly in Germany and partly in the United Kingdom.
At the time of sending this word, however, the government of the United Kingdom was informed that there were some over-all con-
Motions jor Papers

siderations of policy which the Canadian government felt should be communicated intergovernmentally.
In this connection I quote the following from the communication sent the British government:
We hold most firmly to the view that, upon the cessation of hostilities with Germany, Canadian forces should be repatriated from the European theatres as quickly as circumstances will permit. A noticeable number of our troops are now in their sixth year of service overseas. A considerable proportion have now served three years abroad. In any event, the average length of overseas service of Canadian forces must be considerably higher than that of the United States forces. Consequently when fighting against Germany has ended there will be a natural and insistent demand here in Canada, as well as amongst our troops abroad, that they should be brought home in the shortest possible time and certainly with no less despatch than that with which American forces will be returned to the United States.
You are well aware that the difficult problem of sea transportation will continue for a considerable time after the defeat of Germany and that the early repatriation of all our forces, no matter how much this will be desired, will not be possible of achievement. Nevertheless, we must say that it would be both unwise on our part, and misleading to you, were we, at this stage, definitely to undertake to furnish occupational forces for the whole period of military control in Germany.
In these circumstances we take the view that our present decision should be reviewed towards the end of the next fiscal year, i.e., prior to 3.1st March, 1946. By that time much that is now hypothetical should be clearer. We should by then be better able to assess the length of the period of full military control of Germany, the strength of occupational forces which can be provided by our European allies, and the requirements of the Japanese war for manpower and shipping. It is uncertain, moreover, for how long after the fighting ends it will be politically possible to provide Canadian occupation forces in view of the fact that the plans for the control of Germany give the Canadian government no voice in the direction of policy.
It will be noted that this communication was sent in January, 1945-over four months before the war with Germany had ended'-and before questions of procedure and representation in the making of treaties of peace had been finally determined.
In December, 1945, the Canadian government. referring to the statement made in January of that year, namely that it would be necessary' for us to review before the end of that fiscal .year the Canadian commitment to provide one army occupational group of approximately 25,000 and eleven R.C.A.F. squadrons, made representations as follows to the government of the United Kingdom:
The cabinet have now given careful consideration to full reports on the subject submitted by our chiefs of staff. These reports have empha-

sized the serious administrative problems that are involved in maintaining comparatively small forces at so great a distance from Canada.
On the basis of the shipping estimated as likely to be available, it is now probable that the Canadian army overseas, except for the occupation force and administrative staffs, will have been repatriated to Canada by March or April of next year. Until this movement is completed the occupation force can be maintained at full strength without substantial departure from established repatriation priorities and without encountering serious problems with respect to replacements. After that time, however, the retention in Europe of the whole occupation force would create administrative difficulties out of all proportion to the numbers involved. We would, furthermore, expect that by then some of the European allies should be in a position to make a larger contribution to the forces which will continue to be required in the British zone in Germany.
The government have, therefore, decided that, beginning in April next, the Canadian Army occupation force should be progressively reduced on a schedule which would provide for its withdrawal by stages with the object of completing movements from the continent before the end of next summer and repatriating all Canadian Army personnel now overseas by the autumn of 1946.
Accordingly, the staff have been instructed to proceed with plans for the movement of the occupation force to Canada via the United Kingdom and to work out these arrangements in such a way as to permit of the orderly release of Canadian formations in consultation with United Kingdom military authorities.

speechtext:
December, 1945. On January 3, 1946, the Canadian government was requested by the United Kingdom government to reconsider this decision on the ground that the withdrawal of the Canadian forces would inevitably result in the retention of an extra number of forces from the United Kingdom. It was also pointed out that when Canada had withdrawn her forces, the United Kingdom would still have a number of men serving in Germany who would have had as much as five years service.
It was suggested that Canada should keep a Canadian division and elements of the Royal Canadian Air Force in Europe at least until after the spring of 1947.
In his message, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom stated that it was recognized that this suggestion would present considerable difficulties for us but it was well that both governments should not hesitate in making known all aspects of their respective situations.
In reply to his communication of January 3, the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom was informed that our government would not be able to modify the decisions about the withdrawal of the Canadian occu-

Inquiries of the Ministry
pational forces as previously communicated. It was pointed out that these decisions had been reached by the full cabinet after a close review of the problems involved in maintaining a Canadian force in Germany after March 31, 1946.
It will be recalled that at that time, namely January of last year, the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent, the Right Hon. Mr. Gardiner, the Hon. Mr. Martin and officials of the Canadian government were in London attending the inaugural meeting of the United Nations Assembly. The Hon. Mr. Gibson was also in London on other business.
On January 22 a meeting was held between the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom and Mr. St. Laurent and his ministerial colleagues at which the question of occupational forces was fully discussed. A verbal report of this meeting was later given to the cabinet.
On February 13. 1946. the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom was informed that the Canadian government had again reviewed the position of the Canadian contingent in the United Kingdom occupational forces in Germany, having in mind the considerations which were put. forward at the meeting between himself, Mr. St. Laurent and other Canadian ministers who were in London, in January; that, in all the circumstances, we could see no alternative to the course of action communicated in our message of December the 8th, 1915, and confirmed in a message of January the 14th. 1946.
In view of this decision, an announcement became urgent.
The following is the text of the public statement as made on February 15, 1946:
The Prime Minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, announced today that the withdrawal from Germany of the Canadian troops in the occupation army would begin early in April and that, with the present shipping forecast, all troops now in Germany should be back in Canada by September or October.
In making the announcement, Mr. King recalled a statement he had made in the House of Commons on April 4 of last year in which he indicated that from time to time, as considerations of safety and security permitted, reductions would be made in the size of the occupation forces.
At the outset. Canadian participation in the occupation of Germany was a natural development from our participation in the military operations in northwest Europe. Unlike the United Kingdom, the United States, the Soviet Union and France, Canada is not one of the occupying powers and is not a member of the allied control commission. The Canadian contingent has consisted only of one division with ancillary troops in the British occupational zone.
Certain of the other European allies which were not in a position to supply contingents at
the beginning of the occupation are now becoming increasingly able to share in occupation duties.
Now that the greater part of the Canadian army has been repatriated, the maintenance of a small occupation force thousands of miles from home has become increasingly difficult. Aside from grave difficulties in certain aspects of administration, the overhead required to provide headquarters, services, amenities, etc., for the Canadian force is inevitably quite out of proportion to its size.
As has been previously announced, one squadron of the R.C.A.F. will be withdrawn from the occupational force at the end of March, 4946, and the remaining squadrons will be withdrawn on the 30tli June. If satisfactory arrangements can be made, they may be withdrawn prior to that date.
The statement I have made today is, I believe, a true and full presentation of all essential features of this matter, and will, I hope, give to hon. members the information desired.

maintopic: THE KING'S BIRTHDAY TO BE CELEBRATED IN CANADA ON JUNE 9

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: THE KING'S BIRTHDAY TO BE CELEBRATED IN CANADA ON JUNE 9
speechtext: Some days ago the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) asked about the date on which the king's birthday would be celebrated in Canada. The reason for the delay in answering his question was the desire to ascertain His Majesty's wishes in the matter. The government had thought that Monday, June 9, would be the best date, and His Majesty is agreeable to that. Therefore the ninth day of June will be fixed for the celebration of the king's birthday in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a philosophical
principle states that the repetition of an act creates a habit. We all rejoice over the Prime Minister's recovery and we are all glad to see him back in his seat in the house, but we
The Aildress-Mr. P. Gauthier

are not surprised because he is used to defeating his opponents. We have no doubt that with such good training he will also gain the next victory. It is also fitting that I should congratulate the mover (Mr. MacNaught) and the seconder (Mr. Cournoyer) of the address. That will suffice as far as congratulations are concerned because, in my opinion, praise like precious stones is valuable when scarce.
I take the opportunity offered by eight paragraphs of the speech from the throne to discuss the question of external affairs during the present debate. Canada's position among the other nations, the work of her delegates at the united nations organization and her attitude in dealing with the important problems which are constantly increasing in number, especially in Europe, are all matters whose importance should not escape the notice of Canadians.
The time limit imposed upon me by the rules of the house will barely permit me to touch lightly on the important matter of treaties which have or will be signed; it is fortunate that it be so, because my knowledge of those extremely difficult matters does not enable me to expand on them.
I have no intention of creating any discord, but I cannot refrain from deploring the attitude of those nations which have taken the name of "The Big Four", towards the other nations they condescend to call the smaller nations.
These smaller nations include Belgium, whose people in both world wars were downtrodden and massacred; Australia whose brave soldiers were fighting in Europe and in Africa before and while their own country was being bombed and invaded; Canada, which, in addition to the large establishments of her three services, kept abreast of the industrial production of the Big Four and fed millions of needy persons. In August, 1946, Canada had contributed 325 million dollars to the world's bank; France, with a population of 39 million, contributed 450 million dollars; the United Kingdom, one billion 300 million dollars, and the United States 2 billion 175 million dollars. Russia, the most outspoken of the Big Four, had not made any contribution. In addition, our country was one of the first to subscribe to UNRRA. Is not the term "smaller" nation ridiculous to every Canadian?
In my opinion the first mistake committed following the end of the second world war was the exclusion of smaller nations from the peace conference and from the signing of peace treaties. All the members of the house and the whole country have supported the protests voiced by the Canadian government. 
Were we not entitled to more consideration from the United States, France and England after our tremendous contribution to the war which has just ended? Are we to understand that we are farther removed from Europe when it comes to sharing parleys for the restoration of world order, than we are when European countries need our money, our industrial products and our help? The great nations of Europe could well have heeded the advice of our statesmen. During and just after the last war, when this country contributed so generously to the relief of the afflicted and the displaced, those great countries could have been taught that charity begins at home. These would have been counsels of frankness, first, and of disinterestedness.
In paragraph 9 of the Canadian government's statement concerning the peace settlement with Germany, as read in the house on January 30, 1947, we read the following:
The political and psychological defects of the treaty procedure adopted at Versailles in 1919 have long been recognized.
I would add that the procedure adopted for the signing of a treaty with Germany was not better in the case of the other countries. Jouvenel, in his book entitled "From One War to the Next", very aptly describes the atmosphere of the times. In those days the big four were Wilson, Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Orlando. Today Molotov has replaced Orlando. The cake has been cut and the pieces are being handed out according to the will of this council of world ministers. I would say that the situation is even worse for, instead of a representative of a Latin country (strange is it not that a Latin nation should always get the worst of the bargain), we have the representative of a brand of imperialism which no longer has any regard for others, whose arrogance is boundless and whose lack of frankness is glaring. I am not indulging in any vagary when I talk of Russia and the soviet; I am stating facts and actions that belong to the present and not to the past.
In 1918 Foch had requested that the natural barrier between Germany and France, represented by the Rhine river, be closed. He repeated his request on January 10, 1919, before the opening of the peace conference. His argument, although very simple, was most logical. On the east short of the Rhine, he said, from 64 to 75 million Germans, united by common language, culture and philosophy, may congregate at a moment's notice; while on the western shore, 49 million people only are in a position to oppose them. Heroic Belgium is as much interested in these demands as France herself. What will the Big Four do when France insists on this

The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier
natural frontier-if its present leaders are as far-sighter as Foch was-when, besides requesting the establishment of this natural frontier, she asks for the Saar? At this moment, she has long been denied this privilege of an essential nature. In an editorial I read yesterday, signed by Edouard Herriot and published in the Standard, it is stated that none of the big four has yet taken a definite stand on the matter. According to Herriot, however, it seems that Great Britain is ready to allot the Saar to France. Belgium, being among the small nations, could undoubtedly not speak with enough authority to be heard that far. In the so-called small countries, are not great men as numerous, if not more so, than elsewhere? Would the friendship of the United States have been secured without the pre-eminent part played by the Prime Minister of Canada?
In section 15 of the Canadian propositions Foch's ideas are apparent, as far as the German ethnical group is concerned. The following excerpt is even more significant:
The German people have clearly indicated that their experience in the line of autonomous democratic government is not yet sufficient to prevent a centralized state from becoming an instrument of despotism and armed aggression.
May I add that, owing to their peculiar philosophy, based on race superiority, a theory which was imported and implanted by a renegade named Stuart Chamberlain, the Germans will not readily give up their desires, because they are eternal: philosophical ideas do not die; if, at times they seem to disappear, it is only to better readapt themselves. Nazism and fascism are not dead; we have read in the papers about plots discovered very recently in occupied Germany and Austria. And the Italian fascist party comprises already over 300,000 members. The government adds, in the middle of that same paragraph:
For this reason, the German state should be federal in character and not Unitarian. The decentralization of Germany by federalism may become effective and acceptable especially if realized on an economic, as well as on a political basis.
How can the opponents of the Minister of External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) accuse him of being a centralist?
But will the "Big" nations be loathe to consider this suggestion of a small country in which is found, after all, so much foresight, an indication of a profound sense of Europe's economic and political history?
Mr. Speaker, treaties have something else besides defects; some qualities at times become apparent and they can be made to benefit mankind on the distinct condition that they
be not neutralized by the egotism of the great powers, by financial intrigues or by any sectarian hatred. The nations which signed the treaty of Versailles may have been well-intentioned, and other results might have been obtained had not economic interests operated at once against the reasonable claims of some nations. Between the two Great Wars, eighteen conflicts have occurred in the world; they were more or less important, and represented, as it were, fixation abscesses for the draining of the war machine. It is true that treaties have not yet been signed, but fighting is still going on in China, in Indonesia and even in Greece.
As in 1919, there is some talk about reparations. Who shall pay and who shall receive? In 1871, France paid $5,000,000,000 to Germany. In 1919, how much did Germany pay to France and why did she not pay? History clearly shows that the vanquished Germans achieved a victory in the economic field over all their erstwhile enemies, who, at that time, for some reason or other, either concluded that Germany was on the brink of bankruptcy or did not wish to strengthen France too rapidly. We would be blind if we did not perceive the fact that at least three imperialisms are facing each other today. I forgot to say, Mr. Speaker, that in 1919 Soviet imperialism was marking time, because the Soviet revolution had not yet been liquidated; White Russia remained a stumbling block until the day when Stalin, who lacked military experience, but had a keen mind, was made head of the Soviet armies, with the result we know. I do not mention French imperialism, which is merely attempting a revival. British imperialism is now undergoing serious difficulties as we were reminded the other night by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) when he mentioned that Great Britain was calling for the help of the United States in Greece. Should this continue, the Socialists will have as a wonderful achievement the liquidation of the Empire.
I believe that the British people would have been well advised to leave Mr. Churchill and Mr. Eden at the head of their government. The United States and Canada have shown better judgment in keeping in power their present leaders. The British Socialist government received a warning from Mr. Churchill at the time it withdrew its forces from Egypt. The British statesman could already then visualize the Soviet's intentions of encroaching upon the Straits and the Middle East.
During the war, American imperialism has progressed by leaps and bounds but in the
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier

future it will have to muster all its resources in order to survive against the hard-pressing imperialism of the Soviets. I say, Mr. Speaker, that if they are to have an intelligent and consistent policy, all imperialistic countries that have accepted commitments during the war will have to rely on the protection of their armed forces. I am not a supporter of imperialism but since the world, nowadays, must admit its existence, I feel that democratic imperialism must be strong enough to resist the other kind, which aims at destroying the present regime. The most dangerous brand of imperialism is that which is combined, at the economic level, with ideological imperialism.
At the root of world wars, there is a cause, a special one which everyone knows: petroleum. During the last war and ever since it has ended, the big powers have had this matter in mind. I quote the findings of a report tabled in the United States Senate by a special committee which investigated the petroleum resources of the world. The United States have a production capacity of 37 billion barrels; British and Dutch interests, 17 billion barrels; Soviet interests, almost 6 billion barrels; other nations, small and middlesized, 7-8 billions. Obviously, three of the Big Four control the output of petroleum. If a small nation discovers petroleum underground, the big powers immediately seize this mineral product not directly, by government intervention, but through their financiers who hasten to take over those resources. Even with Roumanian wells under her control, Soviet Russia does not yet equal the production of her two rivals, but she brings great care to the expansion of her possessions. The mineral oil found in the Middle East is a cause of turmoil among the big powers and might bring about war in that area, located partly in Africa and partly in Asia. More than half the petrroleum reserves of the world lie in *this distant land which also includes southeastern Russia.
Last year's output in the Middle East reached 365 million barrels. British interests come first, then American and finally French and Dutch. According to newspaper reports, France is claiming new concessions in Irak. Russia, though last to arrive on the scene, has already acquired concessions in northern Iran, thus increasing the considerable output she derives from the Baku fields, which represent 90 per cent of the Soviet Union's petroleum producing resources.
While the great powers are struggling for the possession of the world's petroleum supplies and the establishment of their trade,

they will have to settle the fate of Germany and Austria, a country surrounded by Soviet satellites: Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Yugoslavia. As everywhere else, the Soviets organize before departing. The Allies seem to have secured free navigation on the Danube, a river crossing those countries and the northeastern part of Austria. Under pretext of reparations payments, machines and raw materials have been taken away and have immediately found their way to Russia. The Potsdam agreements do not list the various German and Austrian firms, although they provide that German property will be divided among the occupying powers. For the Soviets, the Austrian properties operated by Germans during occupation are German and must therefore be removed. The Austrian legislature passed an act to nationalize industries previously seized by the nazis, but the Soviet occupation authorities rendered it inoperative. According to President Karl Remner, economic life in Austria cannot be restored without the petroleum and the mechanized industries of eastern Austria. Furthermore, agricultural production has been reduced by half, in this country, by the nazis, in favour of war industries. Then Yugoslavia demands reparations to the tune of 11 billions from Germany and Austria. This will be an interesting problem to solve if Soviet imperialism forces England and the United States to yield. Perhaps, the Big Four may be in need of advice from the smaller nations in matters of this sort.
Let us revert to imperialism. Reparations from the satellites of the axis have been assessed at one billion dollars; the Soviets alone will be getting $100,000,000, over a seven year period from Italy; $300,000,000 in eight years from Roumania; $200,000,000 in eight years from Hungary; $300,000,000 from Finland. Out of a billion dollars, $100,000,000 are left for the others. As our old classics said: Partibus jactis sic locutus est leo.
What are these requests and these demands based on?
Let us cast a glance on the armies of occupation in Europe. The Soviet minister of Foreign Affairs claims that England, France and the United States still have too many soldiers under arms. Here is a table showing the size of the armies of occupation as of October, 1946:

And the Russian foreign minister, Mr. Molotov, says that the other nations have too many soldiers under arms in occupied countries.
Last year, in the debate on the loan oi $1,250,000,000 to Britain, my stand differed from the one I had taken during the war on matters pertaining to billions of dollars. I have not changed my mind as regards the gift, nor about the loans at too low a rate of interest. If I endorsed the last loan, it was because I thought it my duty to support the United Kingdom against an imperialism which is now outstripping it and is becoming a menace for America and the world at large. A man whose opinion is more authoritative than mine, Senator Vandenberg, took the same stand in the United States Senate, during the debate on the American loan of four billion dollars to England. At that time, my apprehension was justified; today, my argument is still stronger.
Let us consider the rise of communism in France since 1922. That year, there were
100,000	communists in that country; in 1936, when the party was dissolved, their number had increased to 1,500,000. In 1945, the number stood at 4,886,000. We must, of course, bear in mind the fact that women now vote, which accounts for a quite considerable increase in the number of communists. At the beginning of 1946, they totalled 5,302,046 and in November of the same year, 5,475,965. That is a geometrical progression. However, France is in Europe; some people may say that it is far away, but France is comparatively near Russia.
Let us come back to our hemisphere in order to consider what is happening in Cuba, a very small country. In 1938, 40,000 communists were to be found there; in 1940, 60,000; in 1946, 150,000, so that within six years communist sympathizers increased by
90,000.	As I was saying, that is the situation in a very small country.
I	said at the outset that Germany's cravings were eternal; let us make no mistake about it,
similar hopes are cherished elsewhere. Czarist ambition had spread Russian power, in 1914, up to a line running from Kolberg, in Pomerania, to Fiume, in Austria-Hungary,
city made famous by d'Annunzio. Czarist ambition included European Turkey and the Asiatic shore of the Dardanelles; thus, Russia opened onto the Black sea, which it dominated as well as the Baltic, and reached the Mediterranean. The area included Russia proper, Poland, Finland, the Baltic states and Bessarabia; the Czarist sphere of influence thus spread to Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary. Roumania, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria and Albania.
In 1939, Stalin began, where the czars had left off, the expansion of Russia through the partition of Poland and the acquisition of the Baltic states at Yalta and Potsdam. The western advance was pushed to the Elba, in the north, and as far as Trieste in the south. Incidentally, I cannot help criticizing the action of Mr. Bidault who internationalized that city instead of leaving it to the Italians. My belief is that Trieste will become a second Danzig, a new Polish corridor. Perhaps Mr. Bidault was influenced by the Communist rise in France. One more Latin nation is left in the lurch, or, rather, is sacrificed. Trieste is in the main Italian; barely one third of its population is of Yugoslav extraction. Instead of satellite kingdoms, satellite republics have been set up in central and eastern Europe. The czars would have been content with stationing troops in Pomerania. The Russian army now occupies all of eastern Germany. How will it be evicted? Northern Bukowina and eastern Galicia are integral parts of Russia which now controls more than the Czars ever did. In one important respect, the Soviets have, until now, fallen short of the Czarist plan.
Turkey still has her European territory, even larger than at the time of the czars, the Bosphorus and Dardanelles. However, you have no doubt noticed that Russian ministers do not fail to mention the word "justice" every time they speak of the Bosphorus and Dardanelles, since they want an interest in the East. The Soviet are still claiming a part in the control of those straits. When they succeed they will have attained the aim set by the czars. But the Soviets have spheres of influence which place them in a better position than the czars. Their sphere of influence comprises Poland, which has her own government, acting only in conformity with Soviet Russia's policies, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Roumania, Yugoslavia, Bulgaria and Albania.
The Address-Mr. P. Gauthier

In Asia, the Soviet sphere of influence is strongly felt in Manchuria, Korea, China, Outer Mongolia, Azerbaijan and Transjor-dania. They have taken from Japan the peninsula of Karafuto, and the island of Sakhalin, which possess enormous reserves in lumber and petroleum.
Around Greece, we have the following satellites of Soviet Russia:	Albania, Yugoslavia and Bulgaria. We must not forget the port of Dairen, in Manchuria, which Russia took over in order to protect Soviet interests in Northern China.
Are we not justified in having fears for the future of democracy, even if Tim Buck did not exist? I will go further:	I am not
convinced that we should share the secret of the atomic bomb. The Baruch plan proposes the inspection of uranium deposits; the Soviets have refused to submit to such inspection. According to La Presse of March 6, Mr. Gromyko has expressed, in the security council, Russia's refusal to abandon her veto right even in regard to the control of armaments. This is very significant. Russia refuses to submit her armaments to the inspection of the united nations representatives. Mr. Andrei Gromyko, Russia's delegate, has informed the council as follows:
(1)	Russia will not allow the inspectors of the international control body to roam freely throughout her territory;
This is nothing new; such has been the case since 1917.
(2)	Russia will not allow an international control body to control her atomic research work;
She has also a source of uranium.
(3)	Russia will not renounce her veto right in matters pertaining to atomic energy.
(4)	"It will be difficult, if not impossible" for Russia to accept the international control of atomic energy, irrespective of the form which it might take, unless the United States agree to destroy existing atomic bombs.
It is likely that that last paragraph led Walter Lippman to believe that Russia might know the secret of the atomic bomb. I do not hold that view.
Let us see where the quest for uranium is taking place.
While ten nations have endorsed the United Nations' plan for the control of atomic energy, it has been rejected by Russia and Poland. Why? Most undoubtedly because it provides for the inspection by the United Nations of territories behind the iron curtain. A great Canadian soldier, General McNaughton, who, as everyone knows, is not given to inconsiderate statements, has advised Canada and the United States to keep up their production. Czechoslovakia is actively prospecting for

uranium. In Saxony, Russian geologists have come across uranium deposits in a discarded lead mine, formerly owned by the Germans. Uranium is to be found in the Urals. India has chlorium, used with uranium. There are uranium deposits in Mexico, Canada and the United States. Argentine has placed an embargo on her uranium. The United States have already invested two billions in the plant that turned out the famous bomb. Russia's stockpile of uranium has increased threefold and Great Britain is spending 200 millions on research.
As a handsome gesture, Russia has put forth the honour system, assuring that every nation would keep its pledge not to use atomic energy in war time. But the Briand-Kellogg pact was based on honour, and we have had war just the same.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish my few remarks,-even though they be but the utterances of a modest member in the parliament of a small nation,-were heard by all the democratic governments of the world. When I say democratic governments, I refer to the true democracies. I said a while ago, that philosophies live forever. If the Big Pour are interested in the economic factors, the psychologic and philosophic elements should arrest their attention to an even greater extent. For a certain brand of imperialism, economic warfare is a corollary to ideologic warfare. A country, Turkey has dared to banish the communist party. This gesture has had and will have in the future happy or unhappy consequences according as it will or will not be seconded or copied by the democracies. My opposition to communism does not spring from mere curiosity to follow its developments or to draw attention to my poor person. It springs from the democratic principles in which I have faith and which I would like to see upheld in the world, through far-sightedness, courage, strength and frankness in the various leaders.
I once more take the opportunity of congratulating our government for the practical propositions they put forward in connection with the preparation of peace treaties with Germany and Austria and I thank them on behalf of my constituents, for the wholly Canadian stand taken by the Minister of External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) in our relations with the whole universe.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a time-honoured debate on the address to be presented in reply to the speech from the throne and the amendments that have been moved to that address. The speech

The Address-Mr. G. Black
from the throne is, in fact, a government statement placed in the hands of the governor general to be read to parliament by His Excellency. The present speech refers to some legislation to be introduced at this session, including old age pensions and readjustment of representation in the House of Commons. As to both these measures, I have something to say, but first I should like to tell the house something of my own constituency, as other members in this debate have told the house of theirs.
The people of Yukon depend entirely on the success of mining for their livelihood. Everything centres on mining. People engaged in merchandising, agriculture, railroading, steamboating, trucking, all manner of transportation; professional people such as lawyers, doctors, nurses, dentists, clergymen; printing houses, aviation, hotels, restaurants, entertainment, government liqour stores, civil servants, could not carry on and could not make that country their home if it were not for the mines producing gold, silver, lead and zinc.
Gold in great quantity was first discovered in Yukon on August 17, 1896, over half a century ago and Yukon's mines are still producing millions.
When the news of that great gold find became known, there was a world stampede to Klondike. People went there from all the countries of the globe, from every province in the dominion and from every state in the union. English, Scotch, Irish, French, Italians, Spaniards, Germans, Australians, New Zealanders, Scandinavians, Japanese, Chinese, Koreans and even East Indians came. Thousands made fortunes, brought them out and, for the most part, settled in Canada and the United1 States. Others failed and came away empty-handed. Many remained to make their homes in that grand north country. It is no overstatement, Mr. Speaker, to say that over $300 million worth of gold has been mined from Yukon, and there are millions now coming out, with more yet to come.
While it is correct to say that in the early days generous grants of money were made by the federal government to Yukon Territory, it is nonetheless a regrettable fact that a large percentage of those amounts was wasted and spent without any beneficial result to the country. Impossibilities were attempted with regard to regulating navigable waters. Roads were built where they could not be used and they had to be abandoned. Eventually capital acquired most of the mines, developed hydro electric power, operating fleets of giant gold dredges and by hvdraulic monitors swept
down hills rich with gold. That was all placer gold torn from the rocks of the mountains by some upheaval of nature and strewn across the country in nuggets and gold dust, as were strewn the rocks in boulders, gravel and sand.
Recently gold in place in veins has been discovered in Yukon, deposits startling in value. Development is well under way and soon these mines will be producing and adding to the wealth of Canada.
About fifty million dollars' worth of silver and lead had been mined in Yukon when, owing to the low' price of those metals, silver mining for a time came to a standstill. Now with better prices, within the past year new Canadian companies have acquired large holdings and are producing ore for shipment. Within a very short time the output should treble what- it formerly was.
The dominion government has had a substantial revenue from the gold and silver mines in Yukon. At first a royalty of ten per cent on gross output of gold was collected, then five per cent, now two and a half per cent. Silver and lead mines pay a graduated tax on profit.
No manufacturing is done in Yukon. Everything used is imported-food, clothing, machinery, hardware, most lumber, all coal, gasoline and liquor. On all those commodities the federal government gets a revenue in customs, excise, sales tax, transportation tax, land tax, recording fees and luxury tax. With regard to the luxury tax, the same luxury tax is imposed on a pack strap as on a bit of jewellery. Far from being a luxury, a pack strap is of necessity an instrument of torture, as anyone who has had to use one will agree.
Yukon's greatest need today is for roads from the mines to railhead, roads for development. Without roads there can be no advance. In some districts in Yukon development is at a standstill for lack of roads. Yukon did have an all-weather road from Dawson, the centre of gold mining, to railhead at Whitehorse, built with money provided by the federal government for that purpose. It was built many years ago. It was first traversed by horse-drawn coaches and sleighs, hauling freight and passengers. Then it was put in shape for motor traffic and was used by motor vehicles, tractors, trucks and automobiles. But for some unaccountable reason the federal government, by its commissioners and controllers, so wilfully neglected that road that it cannot now be used, whereas a relatively small annual expenditure would have kept it in condition and so improved it as to make it a first class unpaved road.
Owing to that policy or shameful lack of policy and common sense, Dawson, which is

The Address-Mr. G. Black
probably the oldest producing placer gold camp in the world, and Mayo, the silver camp, both of which have given and are giving the government substantial revenues, and will continue to do so, are as to transportation in winter, entirely isolated and cut off from the world except for a plane service which can operate only when visibility permits, and which charges freight and express rates that are practically prohibitive.
Let me cite just a few items showing the costs of household commodities which put the cost of living in Yukon sky-high, caused largely by the high cost of transportation on account of the government's neglect of that road to railhead, to which I have just referred. At Dawson gasoline now costs $1.50 a gallon; coal oil, over $1 a gallon: wood fuel-a soft poor quality of spruce-$22 per cord; electricity, twenty-five cents per kilowatt hour, plus government tax. Other necessities of life are proportionately expensive.
The Alaska highway, built through Yukon by the United States, has opened up formerly inaccessible areas. Already deposits of lode and placer gold have been discovered adjacent to it. A steady stream of traffic north and south goes over that road, winter and summer. Unfortunately, it goes nowhere near the old town of Dawson; it is hundreds of miles from that town. But it has certainly put the Yukon town of Whitehorse on the map. It is being kept in good condition by maintenance crews under the management of Canadian army engineers commanded by Brigadier Walsh. But at that, they are under a great handicap in having to use secondhand and worn-out machinery purchased by this government of Canada from the United States; for when the American army moved out and turned control of that highway over to Canada they left very little equipment that was worth having. Stopping-places and filling stations have been built along the road and tourists camps are being built.
I now' come to the reference in the speech from the throne to readjustment of representation in the House of Commons. The bill, if enacted, adds the district of Mackenzie in the northwest territories to Yukon as an electoral district, an impossible proposal. It is so impossible and impracticable that one wonders if those sponsoring the bill are really in earnest. If they are, it show's them to be totally lacking in knowledge of conditions in those areas or willing to discard all proprieties.
It may interest the house to know how those affected territories, Yukon and the northwest territories, are now governed. In Yukon they have an elected council with approximately

the same powers as the legislature of a province. They can legislate as to property and civil rights; they can vote or they can withhold supply. But the government of the territory is carried on and administered by an appointee of the federal government, who is appointed here in Ottawa.
The council of the northwest territories is not elected. It is composed of an aggregation of civil' servants, government employees who are here in Ottawa, thousands of miles away from the people for whom the}' are legislating. Like Yukon, the northwest territories are governed by an official appointed by the federal government.
In neither instance is the government of those territories responsible to the electors, as is the government of Canada, and as are the legislature in the provinces. The estimates for the coming year show a vote of $155,000 for Yukon which, broken down, is shown to be practically all for salaries and remuneration payable to federal employees. There is not a dollar for the development of the resources of that country, not a dollar for transportation. Yet, handicapped as Yukon is by lack of roads, there are those who would add to the political area of Yukon over 500,000 square miles of wilderness.
Let us see how that wilderness, the district of Mackenzie, fares with its government sitting here in Ottawa. I do not begrudge them what they get; I am glad to see them get it. But surely Yukon ought to have equally fair treatment. The government of the Northwest Territories is to get $3,306,000. of which $1,130,000 is for roads. They are to have a water and sew'age system installed at Yellowknife townsite at a cost of $745,000. Whoever heard of a municipal project of that kind being paid for by a federal government? Towns in Yukon have to instal their own water and sewage systems, and the people who use them have to pay for them. But here the federal government makes the town of Yellowknife a present of what is proper!}' a municipal project.
Referring to redistribution. I would predict that before the measure becomes law-

And with all respect I should like to remind the Acting Speaker that this is a matter referred to in the speech from the throne, where it states:
You will be invited to consider a measure to provide for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons.

The Address-Mr. G. Black
It is usual to have termination of the debate on the speech from the throne before matters are referred to committees, so that hon. members may not be handicapped in what they have to say. But at this session we have had the extraordinary procedure of referring the matter to a committee before conclusion of the debate on the address in reply. I do not think hon. members should be handicapped because of that unusual procedure. I hope I shall not traverse too far against Your Honour's ruling.
I predict that before the legislation becomes law, in its present atrocious form-and it is in an atrocious form-the people in the Mackenzie district themselves will protest, and will not submit to being so ruthlessly pushed around. I believe they would prefer to remain unrepresented in parliament rather than have to accept representation on the fantastically ridiculous terms proposed. There has scarcely yet been time to hear from them, but I predict we shall.
With its council of lobbyists, civil servants living here in Ottawa engaged in lobbying the government, whose employees they are, the Mackenzie district has not fared so badly. They induce the government to play Santa Claus to the people under their remote control -very remote control, thousands of miles away. Those people are being well cared for. As I said before, I do not begrudge them what they get; on the contrary I am glad they are getting it.
There is another matter to which I would direct the attention of the house, and I do so in view of the statement made in the speech from the throne:
Progress is being made in overcoming the shortages in building supplies, thereby accel-lerating the provision of additional housing. Despite all obstacles, the number of housing units completed in 1946 approximated the objective set by the government.
The matter I should like to bring to the attention of the house, the government, the minister and his department is the neglect of veterans who returned to their homes in Yukon after the war which ended two years ago. The terms of the Veterans Land Act apply to Yukon just as they do to the rest of Canada. However, in their wisdom the minister and his staff have not seen fit to apply it to veterans of Yukon. Thus far no veteran has been able, under the act, to purchase land in that territory. Under the various housing measures not one veteran's house has been built in Yukon.
When the Veterans Land Act was before the house at the last session neglect of veterans of Yukon was discussed. Let me quote briefly what was then said by the minister and by myself, and the undertaking
which he gave at that time. A question of doubt was expressed as to whether the act applied to Yukon. I read then, and I repeat at this time the wording of section 7 of that act, which states:
The director may for the purpose of this act
(a)	purchase by agreement, at prices which to him shall seem reasonable, or
(b)	in any other manner acquire by consent or agreement from His Majesty in the right of Canada or from any province or municipal authority, or from any person, firm or corporation such lands and buildings situate in any part of Canada and such other property including building materials.-
and so on.
I am sure the house, and the minister administering the act, must know that Yukon is part of Canada. By its wording the act applies explicitly to all parts of Canada.
To remove any doubt in the matter, on August 1, 1946, I moved an amendment by which I would have added a paragraph to the then section 35. The minister then asked me to refrain from pressing my amendment, and said:
I wonder if the hon. member, after having presented his case clearly and convincingly, would be good enough not to press the amendment, with my assurance that I shall be glad to consult with my colleagues at to what can be done to meet the suggestion he has made.
To this I replied:
Under the circumstances I hesitate to press the amendment. To my mind, section 7 is broad enough, in that it gives the director the right to purchase land from any person, firm or corporation-and not only the land, but the land and building situate in any part of Canada.
Then said the minister:
1 have not had an opportunity of consulting with my colleagues in regard to the matter. I would urge that the amendment be not now pressed, and I give the assurance that it will be carefully considered.
Accordingly the amendment was not pressed. But I should like to know now what has become of the careful consideration that was to be given to the matter during the recess, a recess which lasted from August to January 30 this year. The minister has had five months for consideration, five months during which, so far as I am aware, no action has been taken to better conditions of veterans in Yukon, notwithstanding the minister's undertaking given to the house.
Lest the minister is under any misapprehension to the effect that land in Yukon is not available for veterans, I can assure him that investigation would disclose that ample land is available for home sites for veterans. There is no shortage of lumber there, and in Dawson there are a number of large, well built and well preserved vacant government
The Address-Mr. Knowles

buildings which could be dismantled so that the lumber and fittings would be available for building purposes. The speech from the throne stated that the shortage of building material was being overcome. In this way the veterans in Yukon could be housed. I would regret to have to conclude that the reason why nothing has been done for the veterans in Yukon is the lack of interest on the part of the minister, notwithstanding his promised consideration.
I had intended to say something on old age pensions, but there will be ample opportunity when the promised legislation on old age pensions is introduced into the house. Therefore I will defer my remarks until that time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne contains the promise of legislation which is so long overdue that in my view it should have been presented to the house not later than the day after the speech was read to us in the other place by His Excellency the Governor General. I refer to the matter to which the hon. member who has just taken his seat made reference in his closing remarks -old age pensions. I rise at this time to point out that, instead of the immediate attention it should have been made possible for this house to give to this matter, we have been advised that there will be a delay. Our experience with the capacity of the present government for delaying matters is a sad one and I am afraid that, this delay may run into many months. I rise now to protest most strongly and to condemn the government for its delay and to express the hope that it may not last much longer.
The fact is that one can hardly find words adequately to criticize the present government's old age pension policy. To ask our deserving older Canadians, first of all to wait until they are seventy years of age and then if they live that long, to try to exist on a maximum of $25 a month, is shamefully inhuman and utterly callous. When we consider that, in addition to these inadequacies, there is in the Old Age Pensions Act, despite all the protests that have been made against it, a vicious means test; when we realize also that this government has made no provision for medical and hospital care and other things that our older people need, it all adds up to a sorry story of inhumanity and neglect.
To make matters worse, when we reach the point where it becomes necessary for the government to do something we are treated to still further delays. When I refer to reaching a point when something has to be done I have in mind the expiry of the National

Emergency Transitional Powers Act which led some of us to hope that this matter would be dealt with before March 31. Instead of that, when I questioned the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) about the matter on February 4, as recorded on page 83 of Hansard, he indicated that it was the intention of the government to ask for an extension of the present $25 a month beyond March 31, leaving until a later date the amendments to the act which were forecast in the speech from the throne and which we were told would include all that we now have and something more. But wThen that will be done we do not know.
A few days later, on February 10, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) confirmed this policy of delay by indicating, as reported on page 258 of Hansard, that the omnibus bill which he is to introduce will make provision for the continuance of the present $25 basis beyond March 31. In explaining the reason for this delay he said that he felt it was impossible to expect the Old Age Pensions Act to be amended before March 31, and he gave as the reason this could not be done the excuse we have heard in this house time and time again, namely, that the matter is the subject of discussion with the provinces.
We contend that this matter has not crept up upon the government unawares; it is indeed of their own creation. Furthermore, I would point out that on June 24 of last year the then Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Claxton) gave the house a clear-cut promise that the Old Age Pensions Act would be amended in that year, no matter how long the session lasted. A few weeks later, on July 5, the Prime Minister gave an indication of the business to be dealt with, and when I noticed that there was no reference to the Old Age Pensions Act I asked if the promise made by the then Minister of National Health and Welfare would be fulfilled. The Prime Minister replied that he would have to take a look at the promise. A week later, on July 12, as recorded on page 3394 of Hansard, he told us that the government had changed its mind in this matter and had decided to let the old age pensions situation be covered by the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, leaving until this session the amendment of the Old Age Pensions Act itself. The excuse was that other business was more pressing.
In September, 1945, during the first session after the last election, I had something to say about this matter. It was shortly after the dominion-provincial conference in August when the government had made it clear to all the country that it was not satisfied with

The Address-Mr. Knowles
the present old age pension set-up by proposing art increase to $30 a month payable to all over seventy years of age without a means test.
I drew attention to the fact that the figures given for that old age pension plan were all based on the year 1948, and I asked a question which apparently was a bit annoying to the government, whether that meant that 1948 was to be the year of the next election. The then Minister of National Health and Welfare asked for the privilege of interrupting me to answer that question immediately, and he gave as his answer the contention that when the figures were worked out it was thought that 1948 would be the first full year after the war. When I countered by asking him when he thought the increased old age pensions would come into effect his reply was the same old story; he said the new rates would come into effect when there was agreement among the provinces and the dominion.
So we have had this story of delay, this waiting for the provinces right across the years. In the meantime the old people of this country have suffered beyond measure because of the small pittance upon which they have been asked to exist. I am sure hon. members will know from their own experience, as I do, of old people who have passed on sooner than they otherwise might have, simply because they could not keep alive on the amount provided by the government. I suggest that even in the comfort of this chamber we should try to face the meaning of these things in the lives of the human beings who are the victims of the government's constant delay. A terrible responsibility rests upon the shoulders of a government that still continues to give such a small pittance to our old people. Their very lives are in its hands. The time has gone for this continual delay and this continual passing of the buck to the provinces; the time has come when we should deal with the matter right here in this house.
We in this group have been making specific suggestions to the government. Since making those proposals we have received comments on them from one end of the country to the other. Our proposal is that the pension should be raised immediately to not less than $50 a month and be payable at the age of 65. We also insist that the means test be abolished; let there be no doubt about that. We urge also that there be added to the pension where necessary a cost of living supplement which would fluctuate with changes in the cost of living, and also an invalidity supplement. We suggest as well that there should be provided medical, dental, optical, and hospital care for our old people, and further,

that the time has come when this kind of provision should be paid for entirely by the federal government.
Not only have we been getting support on our stand from all over the country, but I was most interested a few weeks ago in the remarks made by a distinguished Canadian when he said that he did not know what attitude the Conservative party would take on this question but that it had been drawn to his attention that the C.C.F. suggested raising the ante to $50 a month and having the pension payable at the age of sixty-five. This distinguished gentleman, after discussing in the course of his speech the estimated cost of various pension plans, went on to say that a large amount of money would be required to pay old age pensions; but "I, for one," said he, "would hate to think that when I reach the age of sixty-five I should have anything less than $50 a month to live on." He went on to say that he liked much better the sound of ten times that amount and he called upon his colleagues-he was speaking in the so-salled other place-to face seriously up to this question of old age pensions, which he insisted could not be brushed aside. These remarks, Mr. Speaker, were not made out on the hustings, nor were they made by someone concerned about getting votes at the next election. They were made by the government leader in the senate. And so, Mr. Speaker, with support like that from the Hon. Wishart Robertson, as well as the kind of support indicated from all over the country, making it very clear that the people of Canada really want to do the right thing by our old people, I rise today to urge the government to put an end to this policy of delay and bring this matter before the house at an early day. There is no need at all to insist on covering the old age pension question in the omnibus bill. All that would mean is that the $25 a month could stay in effect for another year. I call upon the government to bring in its amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act on Wednesday or Thursday of this week just as soon as this debate is ended and let the house have a chance to express its views on the matter, when I am satisfied that members from all parts of Canada, knowing as they do the views of their constituents back home, will support the government in any move it makes, provided that it has in it some touch of generosity, so long overdue.
It is usually the practice of the government, in rising to reply to an appeal such as this, to make a boastful speech about what it has done for our old people and with regard to social security generally. During the last few

The Address-Mr. Knowles
days I have been making a study of old age pension plans and related social security measures in a number of other countries just to see where Canada fits in. The countries whose plans I have studied are nine in number: the United States, the United Kingdom, New Zealand, Australia, France, Czechoslovakia, Sweden, Denmark, and the Soviet Union, and I wish to draw the attention of the government and the house to Canada's position in relation to these other nine countries with respect to various aspects of old age pension plans.
First, let us consider the age. I find that one of these nine countries, Sweden, does not pay its old age pension until the age of sixty-seven, but even that is three years younger than the age at which we pay it in Canada. All the others of these nine countries I have named pay the old age pension at the age of sixty-five or sixty, and in some cases even younger. Only Canada still insists upon her old people waiting until they are three score and ten.
I turn now to the means test. I find that New Zealand has two plans. One is an old age benefit which is subject to a means test, and the other is a universal superannuation, which, has no means test whatsoever. In the United States they have also two plans. As a matter of fact there are more than that, because the plans vary from state to state, but in the main the provision made by the federal government in the United States consists of two plans. There is old age assistance, something like the plan in New Zealand, which is contingent upon a means test, but there is also old age and survivor's insurance without a means test. The United Kingdom, France, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Sweden, and the Soviet Union, have no means test whatsoever. Only Canada, of all these countries, maintains the vicious kind of humiliating means test that we inflict upon our old people.
I hold in my hand a copy of the form that is sent out to old age pensioners in my province once a year, asking for detailed: information of all kinds in reply to twenty-three questions that appear on this form, apart from all the sub-questions. The new income tax form is child's play compared with this document. At the top in red ink appears this statement: "Every question on this form must be answered. Leave no blanks. When completed and verified by statutory declaration mail to-" and the mailing address is given. Underneath that address there is this statement, in red ink and underlined:	"Your pension will
be suspended if this form is not returned properly completed."

The Manitoba old age and blind persons' pensions board, under the means test provisions laid down in the federal act. The minister must not try to imply that this government is not responsible for it, for the responsibility for the means test lies right here in Ottawa. The way to get rid of this kind of thing is for this government to abolish the means test entirely right across Canada.
Furthermore, as I have looked over the pension plans of these other countries I have named I find that there are invalidity supplements, or sickness benefits, or both, provided in all nine countries-all but ours. Only Canada restricts its aged people to the so-called pension, and nothing else. In four countries, New Zealand, France, Sweden, and Denmark, cost of living supplements are provided. And so, Mr. Speaker, the things that we of the C.C.F. are advocating are not new. As a matter of fact I find, for example, that invalidity benefits were provided by as backward a country as Germany even before we had the old age pension, which suggests that there is no room for boastfulness on the part of this government. There are also personal supplements, supplements for children, for housing, benefits for the blind and for orphans, for widows, for miners, for occupational diseases, and so on. I find that in all these other countries their pension plans are integrated into a total plan of social security, and the effect of it is that it is a pension in the full sense of the word. Only in this country is it still a matter of charity and disgrace.
