I shall be glad to lend this material to my hon. friend so that he can study it and support our proposal, as I am sure he will.
What does it all add up to? Simply this, are we in Canada not prepared to organize the work and the production which is carried on by the working portion of our population so that we can provide retirement in decency and dignity, for those who have done their day's work? I believe we are.
During the war, more particularly during the last full year of the war, we had three-quarters of a million men and women out of productive employment in this country. They were in the armed forces doing a particular job, but they were not producing goods and services, and yet the rest of the people who were working were able to provide for that three-quarters of a million all their food and clothing, medical, dental and personal supplies, and, in addition, cash in the form of pay and allowances totalling $985,270,670. In the face of that, I suggest that the government should not tell us that the $560 million which it will cost to pay $50 a month at age sixty-five is prohibitive. If we can take that many people out of production and provide them with the necessities of the job that they were doing in time of war, I submit that we can take fewer people out of production-only 190,000 are being paid pensions today, but the number would be greater if we abolished the means test, although considerably smaller than the first number I mentioned-and provide for their needs quite easily. The cost would be considerably less than what we spent to maintain our armed forces. We can do it, and in the name of humanity we must.
I now wish to deal with another subject. Like the previous one, this is a matter on which my voice has been heard in this chamber before, and it will be heard repeatedly until we get somewhere with it. I refer to the gross injustice perpetrated upon the employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company who were out on strike in 1919. I have told the story fairly often so that I need only summarize it briefly.
At the time of the 1919 strike the pension plan then in effect was a non-contributory one. Those who oppose me in this matter seem to like to point that out. I have pointed it out since the first time I raised the matter in the house. It was non-contributory, but evidence is conclusive that down through the years the men were told, particularly every time there was any discussion on wages, to 83166-78
remember that when they were working for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company they were working not just for the wages they received but also for the pension they would have at the end of their days of labour. As a result of this, the men were led to believe that they had a definite equity which was being built up through the years. However, when the men went back after the strike in 1919 they discovered that the company took the view that that strike had been a break in service, and therefore unilateral and arbitrary action was taken by the company in saying that the men who were over forty years of age could not enjoy their pension rights at all, and the men who were under forty, though they were permitted to re-enter the company's pension plan, were denied all the rights they had earned up until 1919. At that time about five hundred employees were affected to the extent of 100 per cent. That is, there were about five hundred who were over forty years of age and who therefore lost all their pension rights. There were another 2,200 or so who were under forty. These 2,200 were permitted to enter into the pension plan again, but they lost the rights they had earned prior to 1919.
It was a long story from that time down through the years. I refer to the efforts of the men to have this wrong righted. Finally, in 1937 a new pension plan came into effect on a contributory basis. The clause that had been used against the men in 1919 was kept in the new plan and it is still in effect. I will not discuss that, since it comes up under another matter, namely, Bill No. 24 which I have introduced and which I hope will be passed later in this session. But despite the efforts made by the representatives of the men at the time the new plan was brought into effect, the company still stood adamant in its refusal to reinstate the rights of men who were out in 1919. I first raised the matter in the house in 1944, and have had a good deal to say about it since that time.
In 1945 the government finally met us part way by appointing Mr. H. S. Johnstone of the Department of Labour as an investigator. The purpose of Mr. Johnstone's investigation was to determine whether or not the government should establish a royal commission to go into this matter. Mr. Johnstone made a thorough study and an exhaustive report, which was presented to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) on December 7, 1945. After some months of pretty hard pulling on our part, we had this report tabled in August, 1946. The report is an exhaustive one. Mr. Johnstone saw all the people concerned on both sides of the dispute and also saw people who were not

The Address-Mr. Knowles

involved in this dispute, but who had been involved in similar problems in 1919, such as the Canadian National Railways, the city of Winnipeg and other employers who reinstated the pension rights of their employees long ago.
After making a full study of the question, and bearing in mind the purpose of his appointment by the Minister of Labour, Mr. Johnstone made a definite recommendation in these words, found on page 17 of his report:
It is the opinion of the undersigned that the employees have established strong claims for consideration. The nature and extent for adjustments, if any, cannot be determined except by a more exhaustive analysis than was possible, or even contemplated, in this preliminary investigation. I would therefore recommend that a royal commission be established to examine into the whole question, to determine what if any consideration should be granted, and if so, then to whom and in what manner pension adjustments should be made.
Armed with a recommendation such as that, the unions concerned have pressed for the appointment of a royal commission, and I have supported their representations in the house as strongly as I could. But the Minister of Labour, speaking for the government in this matter, has repeatedly told us that it cannot be done. The last time the Minister of Labour spoke on it was in reply to a question of mine on the orders of the day on February 3, which is recorded on pages 35 and 36 of Hansard. On that occasion he gave three reasons for not proceeding with the recommendation made to him by an officer of his department. His three reasons were these. First of all, he said that he did not believe in spending the other fellow's money. He said that this was money of the C.P.R.; that the plan was non-contributory and that he felt he should not be put in the position of being asked to spend another fellow's money. In the second place, he said that he felt this was the sort of matter which should be fought out between the unions and the company.

With regard to the first remark, namely that the minister does not like spending other people's money, may I say, first of all, that a

great amount of the people's money, money out of public funds, has been given to the C.P.R. I understand that, across the years, cash grants from the federal government to the C.P.R. have amounted to $89,671,000. In my view, therefore, the people of Canada have some interest in how the C.P.R. spends its money, not to mention the fact that it makes all its money out of the people of Canada. But, in addition to that, the whole question as to whether these men have an equity which is theirs, upon which they have a claim, is basic in the entire dispute, and Mr. Johnstone went into that matter fully. This was his summing up, as found at page 15 of his report:
Any established plan of this nature, whether wholly company-contributory ot not, when maintained for a time becomes one of the established working conditions, and together with the actual wage paid they form the remuneration earned by the employee. The employee argument therefore, that by each year of service he is building up deferred earnings in a pension, is one which has considerable weight. To be deprived of these past earnings by reason of absence on strike or absence during a strike, does not seem to be equitable treatment; and all the more so when the decision is made by the party which will thereby save large sums of money as a result of rigid adherence to this rule.

Thank you. I submit therefore, Mr. Speaker, that the position taken by the minister is not valid. This money is, in part, money supplied by the people of Canada and definitely is the money of the employees who built up an equity, and the Canadian Pacific Rail-way Company has no right to expropriate it arbitrarily and by unilateral action.
As for the minister's suggestion that this matter should be taken up between the unions concerned and the company instead of being brought to the floor of parliament, I have received a number of letters since he made that statement, letters from top-ranking union men in Canada. One of these letters I hold in my hand and it typifies the way in which the men concerned take issue strongly with the minister. Here is a reference to the minister's remarks which I have just quoted:
Does he not know that the question has been the subject of discussion between the parties themselves? Is he unaware that it has been handled by the men's represenatives up to and including the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway? Because we did not receive any consideration from the mighty Canadian Pacific Railway, the question is now before the elected members of the dominion parliament to ascertain if the citizens of the dominion, in this instance, cannot receive justice to which they are entitled? God help them! Where else can they look for assistance but to those who in the

The Address-Mr. Knowles
legislative assembly are elected to see that justice prevails to all citizens of the dominion of Canada, and not only to the privileged classes?
It is because I have received letters like that, because of my contacts with the men-

I am sorry; I was going to mention that. It is signed by J. J. Hendrick, vice-president of the brotherhood of railroad trainmen. It is because of support like that, because of what I know to be the feeling of the men themselves that their case should be brought into the high court of parliament, that I have pressed the matter here repeatedly, and I shall continue to do so until justice is done.
The third remark made by the minister was that no useful purpose would be served by appointing a royal commission. That, it seems to me, is a case of passing judgment in advance, which he has no right to do. There has been a definite recommendation from an officer of his department that a royal commission be appointed. There have been repeated expressions of sympathy by the minister, by the Prime Minister and by members on all sides of the house, and it does seem to me that the fair thing for the government to do would be to carry out this recommendation.
If there are difficulties in the way of appointing a royal commission; if some other form of commission, it is felt, should be appointed, I am sure the men would settle for a different name. But certainly they feel that some kind of public inquiry should be held so that the facts of the matter can really be brought out and a finding made. Whether it could be made compulsory by the government is a matter the lawyers can argue about, but certainly if a public commission were to make the kind of finding that would be given if we had an inquiry by an impartial commission, it would have effect in the eyes of the public.
I mention in passing, as has been mentioned in the course of this debate, that at this time when the C.P.R. is asking, along with others, for increases in freight rates, this matter must be set alongside that request-this treatment that the company has given to these men. But I press home the point that right now the responsibility rests upon this government and upon the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister, who has taken an interest in this matter, to see that this commission is set up.
It is true that the government was not the guilty party in the first place; it was the C.P.R., but the men have appealed to the high court of parliament for action. Their unions have asked for a commission, and an impartial investigator has recommended it. I 83166-781
submit, therefore, that the responsibility now rests upon the government and particularly upon the Minister of Labour and the Prime Minister to see to it that this recommendation is carried out.
I have here a copy of a well-known book entitled "Industry and Humanity" by W. L. Mackenzie King, and at pages 347 and 348 there are a few observations about protection for people in their old age. This was written in 1918 and, as a matter of fact, it bears upon both the subjects I have been talking about, old age pensions and these friends of mine in the employ of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The sentence I wish to read is this:
If lifelong public service in industry is _ to receive its fitting reward, years that are denied opportunity of employment should not be subjected to the humiliation of dependence on charity.
I think, Mr. Speaker, of the plight of the old age pensioners generally, and I am thinking just now of the plight of these employees of the C.P.R., men who have given lifelong public service in industry, men who have served the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for thirty, forty and fifty years, and whose only reward in their old age is the humiliation of dependence or charity.
The Prime Minister said in 1918 that this should not be allowed, and I call upon the Prime Minister now to have a royal commission appointed to go into this matter see that justice may yet be won for these men; for I am satisfied that never was a case pleaded in which justice was so clearly on its side. The responsibility for the continued suffering of these men and their families rests quite clearly on the government.
There are two or three minutes left before my time expires and I wish to refer to one other group of elderly people. I have spoken about old age pensioners generally and I have spoken about the men of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I now wish to say a word about the widows of veterans of the first world war. Hon. members who were here in the last parliament will recall the long struggle to get some kind of allowance for widows of non-pensioned veterans of the first world war. It was quite a story, the way these women came here a few years ago, their perseverence, the difficulties they had, but finally their success in having their case considered, to the point that in 1943 they were granted, if in necessitous circumstances, $20 or $25 a month. A year later, in 1944, this amount was raised to the sum of $30.41 a month, which corresponds with the maximum amount payable as a burnt-out pension under the War Veterans Allowance Act. Since that
The Address-Mr. Knowles

time there has been no appreciable change in the position of these women. The only change of note was made last year when these provisions were made statutory rather than subject to an annual vote. It is still true that the amount is only $30.41 a month, and that the allowance is subject to a rigid means test. Widows of veterans who did not get beyond England in the first world war are not covered at all.
Only a night or two before I left Winnipeg to come here for the opening of the session in January, the last group of people I met before leaving home was an association .of these women in Winnipeg. I wish it were possible, Mr. Speaker, to transplant into the comfort of this green chamber, with all the red roses we have around today, the pitiful circumstances of these widows of veterans of the first world war who are trying to exist on the amount that is given to them. I plead for further consideration of their case, for raising the amount to at least $40 a month, letting down the barriers of the means test, providing hospitalization and medical care for them. Not to do these things is an insult to the memory of their husbands who fought in the first world war. One of the things, which has bothered me has been the change in the attitude of many hon. members about this matter. Back in the days before anything had been done, there was considerable agitation. Members of all parties were rising in their places and pleading the cause of these women. But somehow or another, since they got their $30.41 a month, there seems to be a general tendency to assume that the problem is settled. I have heard members of the official opposition even congratulate the government and compliment them on what they are doing for these widows. The government does not deserve any compliments at all for asking the widows of veterans of the first world war to live on $30-41 a month. I call upon the government to do something about this matter, and I call upon my fellow members in all parts of the house to support me in this plea. Let me put it in this way: let us make nuisances of ourselves about this matter again, and let us see if we cannot get something done this year.
I see that my time has gone, Mr. Speaker, and I must close. I have confined my remarks to these three groups of people, old age pensioners generally, the retired employees of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company who have no pension, and the widows of veterans of the first world war. All of them are victims of inhumanity and callousness; they are also victims of other matters that I could discuss, such as housing shortages, price increases,

and all of that. But enough for now. Just this I desire to say. These people, and indeed Canadians all across this country, are putting a very simple question to the government these days. The question has to do with that new order about which there was so much talk during the war. The question is a very simple one, but straight to the point: Where is it?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), I do so because I believe that the adoption of the measures contained therein is essential in order that we may achieve those things for which we fought, namely an optimum standard of living for our people, with a maximum degree of personal freedom. Canada's great war effort is still fresh in our minds. But let us not forget that the sacrifices which were made during the war were made not merely for the purpose of defeating Hitler, Mussolini and Hirohito, but in order that we in this country may remain free people.
During the war the people were encouraged by promises regarding a new social order and by the declaration of principles known as the Atlantic charter, under which all people might enjoy security and freedom. But let us constantly keep in mind the fact that victory over the enemy was merely the first objective. The ultimate objective is still to be won. We have often been told that the reason the people put forth such a tremendous effort during the war was that they had the incentive to defeat the enemy; that in peace time that incentive is lacking, and that therefore in peace time they will not be prepared to make the same kind of effort as they were in war time, to reach their peacetime objective.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, under dynamic leadership in Canada it should be possible to arouse enthusiasm to attain that main objective of giving to the people of Canada the highest standard of living that the country can produce or the people may desire. Whilst it may take many years to reach that objective in so far as many countries of the world are concerned, nevertheless it can be reached, I believe, at an early day in Canada, thereby giving leadership by example to the other nations of the world.

The Address-Mr. Quelch
And to those people who are so afraid of communism and socialism I would say that the only way to stop their growth in Canada is to make private enterprise work, not merely in the interests of this class or that class, but in the interests of all the people of Canada. However, when I read the speech from the throne I find) no sign of the type of leadership that is essential to inspire people with a will and confidence to drive on to an objective. There can be no security for people who are physically incapacitated, when no provision is made for payment of a pension. There can be no security for the aged on a miserable pittance of $30 a month, or less.
I am aware of the fact that the speech from the throne does mention that an amendment will be passed; but recalling what was said by the then Minister of National Health and Welfare at the end of the last session I have grave doubts as to whether that amendment will bring about the changes in the Old Age Pensions Act which we consider essential. I would say there can be no security for people in the lower income brackets while the government confiscates a large part of their income. There can be no sense of security for workers in this country when they are continually being warned of the danger of approaching depression. How can we expect industry to go full steam ahead when they have no assurance regarding future markets?
As I said, there is nothing in the speech from the throne to inspire people with confidence regarding the future. Again I would remind the house of the warning that was issued to the country by Mr. Graham Towers in his report of 1946. I put it on record last year, but I make no apology for placing it on record again at this time, because it is a warning that should be kept constantly before the people of Canada. I refer to page 9, where I find this:
Clearly it is the first two items in the expenditure table, comprising total government outlay, which represented the main driving force behind the very high level of activity which was attained during the war period. Canada's problem now is to expand the other types of expenditure, and particularly domestic private investment and domestic consumption, in order that there will be compensating stimulus as government outlays decline to their post-war level.
And on page 10:
Looking to the future, however, there is no reason for complacency. Most of our real problems of post-war adjustment are still ahead. The backlog of demand will not be large in relation to productive capacity when industry has been fully reconverted and inventories built up to normal levels. When the time lag involved in demobilization is over, government expenditures will fall rapidly. Nor will our foreign lending to finance the purchase of Canadian
goods remain indefinitely at the present level. The prevailing optimism on the North American continent is dangerous if it diverts attention from the problems which have to be faced.
Many similar warnings have been issued. I should like to refer briefly to a book which I believe most hon. members have seen. It was written by Mr. W. H. Moore, a former member of the House of Commons, andi is entitled, "Grey Days". At page 5, he speaks about a report of a committee of the league of nations, and states:
That world depression should be brought to an end and never happen again the assembly of the league of nations, October 1937, arranged that a delegation of scientists should study the conditions that bring about depression and report on measures to prevent them. After prolonged study the committee issued its report in two sections, the first one in 1943 and the second one in 1945.
I he final report contains 319 pages from which, at present, I extract but six words. After reciting the conditions that led up to the disastrous decade of the nineteen-thirties, the delegation reported: "That history is repeating itself today."
Then I noticed a press report the other day which quoted Mr. L. B. Pearson, under-secretary of state for external affairs, as warning that, unless Canada is careful and lucky, she may be looking back on 1947 with nostalgic envy.
In view of that type of warning, is it any wonder that the people of Canada are becoming leery as to what the future may hold for them? I do not doubt for one moment that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) will be careful-careful not to commit himself to anything definite. That attitude, however, does not help create confidence or inspire the people with enthusiasm. I think it must be obvious to all who seriously address themselves to this problem, that the great danger in the near future will be a depression on account of lack of purchasing power, or lack of effective demand against those goods which the people desire and can be produced in abundance. To a very large extent it will be a repetition of what we in this country suffered during the thirties. I have in mind especially the period of 1935 to 1939. It will be recalled that during that time we had in the neighbourhood of a million people on relief, industry running at less than fifty per cent of its capacity, and half a million unemployed.
During that time it was the common practice to blame industry for that situation. People said, "Why does industry not have more confidence and expand production, utilizing the unemployed to produce goods that the people so sorely need in this country?" I would say that industry was not to blame for that situation. Industry knew only too well that if

The Address-Mr. Quelch
they were to expand their production they would merely have an increased amount of production remaining unsold on their hands, unsold because they were already at that time with that limited amount of production having a great deal of difficulty in disposing of their goods.
The hon. member for Peace River explained in his speech the cause of this situation, namely, that owing to certain practices inherent within the capitalist system industry is not able to distribute sufficient purchasing power in the form of salaries, wages and dividends to make it possible for the people to buy their production except in times of abnormal capital goods construction such as exist in war time or in the early development of new countries. In both these last two cases the purchasing power of the people is maintained by going steadily farther into debt.
As a result of that we are faced with one of three alternatives if we desire to maintain the full development of the resources of the country. We have to export our surplus goods and maintain a favourable balance of trade as was done by the industrialized nations in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, or we have to destroy production on a grand scale as was done in 1930, or we have to adopt the only sane plan, of expanding the purchasing power of the people to the point Where they can buy the total production of the country.
In the past, industrialized nations have tried to maintain employment by the first two means, by exporting their surplus goods and not bringing back imports in return. As the hon. member for Peace River pointed out, that was the policy of England for 200 years prior to 1914. It was true that England maintained a fairly high degree of employment in that period; it is true that, generally speaking, England was considered to be a prosperous nation, but do not let anyone forget that during that period there was horrible distress and destitution among many classes of people in that country.
That situation came to an end to a very large extent in 1914 when the crisis developed. What had happened was that the countries to which England had been exporting goods had themselves become industrialized and were trying to do the same thing; they were trying to export their products to other countries and a tariff war ensued. That policy must be condemned on the ground that there can be no justification for exporting more than you import when that production is sorely needed by the people of the country.

I would say that under no consideration whatsoever can the destruction of goods be justified.
These policies I think are adopted chiefly because of a false objective, the objective of full employment instead of the democratic objective of an optimum standard of living for the people of the country. If your objective is an optimum standard of living, then by no possible means could you justify exporting more than you import, nor would you dream of destroying goods, nor would you reduce production just because there was inadequate buying power to make it possible for the people to buy it. Therefore, in order to achieve that objective you must expand the purchasing power of the people to the point where they can buy the total production of the country. I should like to quote from a report by Doctor Harold Loeb, who was chairman of the national survey of .potential production capacity in the United States in 1935. He was appointed by Mr. Hoover and in his book "Chart of Plenty" under "Conclusions" on page 161, he has this to say:
It would seem that the simple and obvious way out, that of giving a buying power adequate to procure desired goods and services to the limit of our ability to produce them, might well be tried. It is simple in principle but has not been attempted.
It is in the light of this situation that we moved the amendment which is now before the house. Before proceeding, I should like to read the first two sections to which I intend to direct my remarks:	They are:
Ministers ought to have advised Your Excellency that they would introduce in the present session measures providing for:
A.	The return to parliament of complete and effective control of Canada's financial policy.
B.	The use of the national credit to meet at least some of the financial requirements for essential services; and, as a guarantee that this country shall not again be subjected to financial depression, to make available to each and all Canadian citizens a proper portion of purchasing power which shall not first pass through the usual channels of industry, this on a basis calculated to maintain a balance between effective purchasing power in the hands of consumers and the aggregate of the prices of goods available for sale.
We realize that we are still in a transition period and that it is not yet possible to meet all the demands of the Canadian people. However we believe that the standard of living of the people could be greatly increased it we were to remove some of the obstacles in the way of production; if we were to remove some of the heavy taxation and also some of the controls; if were to start and curtail the size of some of the large foreign loans that have been made in the past.

The Address-Mr. Quelch
Nevertheless we are rapidly approaching the situation referred to by Mr. Graham Towers in his 1946 report. I would say that we cannot afford to wait until that situation develops because, once a depression comes into being, it is too late. You have then started to destroy the confidence of the people and it would not be an easy thing to revive production in the country.
Therefore we urge that the following steps be taken. We urge the setting up of a competent national monetary authority operating in conjunction with the Bank of Canada and responsible to the people through parliament. This authority should exercise full and effective control over the operation of the monetary system, including the issue and withdrawal of all currency and credit. This authority should be required to maintain a proper accounting of the national economy to ensure (a) that adequate monetary facilities are available to finance all required production, having due regard to a proper balance being maintained as between capital goods and consumer goods production; and (b), that at all times the people possess effective purchasing power equivalent to the total prices of goods available for sale.
It would also be the responsibility of this national monetary authority to finance all government expenditures that could not be met by an equitable system of taxation, and at the same time without increasing the national debt. Keeping in mind the fact that the real objective of the people is an optimum standard of living and that the main obstacle to achieving this objective in the future will be a lack of effective demand, it should be the responsibility of this financial authority to maintain a balance between the total national consumption, including capital depreciation and exports, on the one hand, and the total national production, including capital appreciation and imports, on the other.
Until such time as production has been expanded sufficiently to take care of the desires of the Canadian people and keeping in mind the necessity of giving assistance to distressed countries, our first job should be to guarantee security for the aged and incapacitated and all those people who are unemployable. It is all very well to talk about a new social order, but first of all let us set our own house in order. There is an old saying that charity should begin at home. Surely Canada with a population of only eleven and a half million to twelve million people and an income of around $10,000 million, an average of about $3,500 per family of four, can do better than a mere pittance of $30 a month for her aged people.
We have urged that pensions should be paid at the rate of $50 a month at the age of sixty; that a similar amount should be paid to all people who are incapacitated and unemployable and that no means test shall be applied. We also believe that the war veterans allowance to both veterans and their dependents should be increased to a similar amount.
In order to ensure that the people of Canada would at all times be able to buy the goods that are offered for sale, the price of these goods should be adjusted so that they bear the same relationship to their financial cost as the total national consumption bears to the total national production. For example, if the financial authority upon checking the relationship between demand and supply find that demand was equal to, say only ninety per cent of the supply, the authority would authorize the payment of a ten per cent discount. The retailers would then sell their goods at ten per cent discount and submit their sales slips to the banks and be compensated for that ten per cent loss; the banks would present their slips to the financial authority and receive credit for the amount they had advanced to various retail merchants, and there would be no increase in taxes. In this way demand would be balanced with supply, and industry could expand with confidence, knowing there would be a ready market for all the goods they produced of a desired quality. As our production steadily expands and the situation referred to by Graham Towers becomes more evident, we could either increase the amount of the discount or, on the other hand, guarantee a basic income to all people. That, of course, would be issued on the basis of the surplus goods which were available for distribution. Surely this would be a far better way of dealing with our surplus goods than destroying them or making foreign investments, and, on the other hand, better than reducing production owing to inadequate buying power on the part of the people. If, by any chance, the guaranteed basic income established was so high that it created a demand greater than could be satisfied, the discount in that event would turn into a sales tax and the balance between demand and supply would be restored in that way.
Some people say, why could we not expand the purchasing power of the people by expanding wages? Unfortunately, when you expand wages you expand costs, and when you expand costs you expand prices, so that the purchasing power of the people will not be increased in relationship to the total prices charged. I quite realize that there would be certain cases
The Address-Mr. Quelch

where wages could be increased without increasing prices, but generally speaking it must be true to say that a general increase in wages brings about a general increase in costs and a general increase in costs brings about a general increase in prices. Therefore, in order to expand the purchasing power of the people in relation to the prices of the goods for sale, additional purchasing power would have to be paid to the people without its passing through the channels of industry. Otherwise it would incur costs in the process, and the purchasing power of the people would not be increased in relation to the total prices of the goods charged.
No doubt some hon. members would say that an increase in purchasing power or a price adjustment is bound to bring about an increase in taxation. Obviously these payments cannot be made by an increase in taxation because that would defeat the very purpose of issuing the purchasing power and decrease the demand for goods. Obviously these payments cannot be made by an increase in the sales of bonds to the people because that would also reduce the purchasing power of the people. I think the war policy proves that point conclusively. It will be recalled that during the war we had very heavy taxation and that we indulged in heavy borrowings from the people, and one of the reasons given for that policy was to curtail the spending power of the people. If heavy taxation and bond sales curtailed! the spending power of the people in war time it is bound to have exactly the same effect in peace time.
I should like to quote from a speech made by the deputy minister of finance, Doctor W. C. Clark, in 1942, at Montebello, as reported in the Financial Post. Dealing with this question, Doctor Clark said:
The same philosophy which has led to these very high taxes in war time is likely to dictate a reversal of that policy in the post-war years. Today, demand is far in excess of supply. Consumer purchasing power is far in excess of the available supply of consumer goods and services. The taxing authorities therefore must through high taxes siphon off as much as possible of that surplus purchasing power if we are to avoid all the evils of inflation.
On the other hand, the post-war period is likely to pose an entirely different set of conditions. If we may judge by the record of the past, we are likely to see, after a temporary period of dislocation and hesitation followed possibly by a consumer goods purchasing boom, a period during which, unless the state acts aggressively and intelligently to prevent it, supply or potential supply may tend to be far in excess of effective demand.
What will then be needed is to safeguard against deflation, not to prevent inflation. If we are to avoid a long depression and mass unemployment, the policy required will be one of stimulation of the economy, one that will

create expansionist tendencies, one that will provide incentives to expansion of production, one that will encourage the consumer to spend and expand his purchasing power, in short, one which will keep the national income from falling to abnormally low levels.
I think that is a warning we can very well take to heart at the present time. So quite obviously that problem cannot be solved through spending money obtained either by taxation or by borrowing the savings of the people, because that in itself is a deflationary policy. The money needed to maintain an effective demand against our production should be issued by the monetary authority. It should be paid direct to the consumer without passing through the channels of industry and would be debt-free, because obviously you cannot meet a deficiency of purchasing power by going into debt; otherwise when the debt is repaid the deficiency would recur.
Former ministers of finance have charged that issuing national money would be highly inflationary because it would increase the cash reserves of the chartered banks and they would then be in a position to expand their loans in the ratio of ten to one of their cash deposits. I think that proves conclusively that we have not effective control over the issue of credit on the part of the chartered banks when we as a nation are placed in the ridiculous and helpless position of not being able to issue our own money without fear of the action of a subordinate body.
Therefore, in order that effective control may be established over the actions of the chartered banks in creating money, we suggest as one means the adoption of the 100 per cent system. We are not dogmatic on this question. We quite realize that there may be many other methods by which the results desired may be achieved, but we suggest that this is one means of overcoming the objection raised by ministers of finance to our suggestion that national money should be made use of to make, up a deficiency in purchasing power. That is to- say, we urge that the Bank Act be amended so that the chartered banks will be required to maintain 100 per cent cash reserves behind their demand deposit liabilities. A national monetary authority could provide the banks with this extra cash by buying from them the dominion securities now held by the banks. Banking would then become wholly a business of lending and reinvesting pre-existing money. The banks would no longer be able to create money as they have done in the past. There would, of course, have to be a sharp distinction drawn as between savings and demand deposits. The savings would be term investments and would be withdrawable only on

The Address-Mr. Quelch
notice. In the past the Minister of Finance has taken the stand in the house that by banks surrendering interest-bearing securities for cash they would have to operate at a loss. I would say that this point has never been proved largely because the government have seen fit to refuse to disclose to hon. members the size of the banks' hidden inner reserves. Nevertheless, if the government or the banks can prove that such a proposal would mean that they would operate at a loss, then the national monetary authority could lend the banks money against their securities instead of buying them outright, and they could be charged a nominal rate of interest on the money advanced to them in that way.
May I point out that this proposal known as the 100 per cent system has been endorsed by many prominent economists and bankers. The 100 per cent system would undoubtedly effectively control inflationary action on the part of the chartered banks. I am not quite satisfied myself that you could also control the danger of a deflationary policy by them.
It is interesting to note what Major Douglas has said on this point. Some people believe that the safest way to establish control over the chartered banks would be by nationalizing them. We of this group have never taken a stand against the nationalization of the chartered banks; we have merely pointed out that you will accomplish nothing by merely nationalizing the banks unless you change their policy. In his book entitled, "The Use of Money", at page 29 Major Douglas points out that, whilst the majority of bankers would be quite prepared to cooperate, nevertheless approximately five per cent at the top would in all probability oppose the adoption of a sane monetary system. Then he goes on to say:
I do not say that something like the nationalization of banking will not have to come. I think it probably may have to come. But what I am perfectly certain of is that if you unite the powers of government with the powers of banking before you have changed the banking system, you have got a problem which is doubly difficult to solve.
In closing, I should like to say to hon. members who are still suffering from the delusion that governments have to depend upon the receipts from taxation and borrowing from the people for their revenue, that that is not how we financed the last war. It is true that we had heavy taxation and large bond sales, but let not hon. members forget that over S3,000 million were created by the chartered banks for the use of the government. In all, over $4 billion of new money was created during that period. Therefore do not let anybody 83166-79
jump to the conclusion that we financed the war solely by bond sales to the public and taxation. We would have had a very different kind of war effort from the one we had if that had been done. The only exception that we would take to the method adopted by the government is that this money was created by the chartered banks instead of by the Bank of Canada. Had it been created by the Bank of Canada, then we would have had that much less debt in the country.
Let me recall the situation which we had in the country back in 1935 and 1939. Hon. members will remember that on every occasion when we in this comer urged the government to use national money to meet the needs of the people we were met with the cry that such a policy would mean inflation. Then the war came, and immediately the chartered banks were hired to create hundreds of millions of dollars in order to maintain the full development of the resources so as to have the greatest possible war effort. We say that if it is possible to create money in wartime to maintain the full development of the resources of the country, then it should also be possible to create money in peace time in order to achieve the objective that we fought for, namely a high standard of living with maximum degree of personal freedom for the people.
It was the declared policy of the government in war time that no financial restrictions should be allowed to impede our war effort. The only limits were the men and materials available. Then we come to the year 1946 and the question of the old age pension is raised in the house. It is suggested that old age pensions of $50 a month at age of sixty should be paid, and once again as from 1935 to 1939 we are met with the same old cry that it cannot be done because it would cost too much money. If, instead of our talking about old age pensions, the war had been on ahd we had been suggesting that we should build, we will say, so many tanks, would we have been met with the cry, we cannot do it because it would cost too much? No; it would have been merely a question of whether or not we had the men and materials to build these tanks. Surely, then, when we are dealing with the question of old age pensions the only thing we should have to consider is whether or not we can provide the goods to satisfy the demand created by the payment of increased old age pension. In view of the fact that we are being warned that the main obstacle which we have to face in the future is lack of effective demand, a very good way to create the demand will be by paying old age pensions to the old people, and paying pensions to all people who

The Address-Mr. McLure

are physically incapacitated. I do not believe *that people will tolerate that kind of financial dictatorship in the future. Let it not be said that money can be the servant of the people only in war, and that in peace time it has to be the master.
Mr. W. CHESTER S. McLURE (Queens): Mr. Speaker, before beginning my address on the speech from the throne, permit me for a few moments to say something with regard to the pleasurable event we had here this afternoon. I am referring to the unanimous welcome extended to our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he returned to his duties in the house. It was a unanimous welcome, and I therefore would make a suggestion that, should it ever occur again, the red roses might be given to both sides of the house.
I should also like to say that during the absence of the Prime Minister the house was most capably led' by the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). Again, sir, it is my privilege to address you as the honourable Speaker of the house, notwithstanding the rumours which have been floating around. Another press report I read-no doubt you have seen it on many occasions yourself-was that a prominent place in the cabinet awaits you when the second shuffle begins. speechtext:
In speaking in this debate, I would be remiss in my duty if I did not congratulate the mover of the address, the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacNaught). He excelled himself as he freely and fearlessly expressed his views, which would be, of course, in accord with those of his own government. The hon. member for Prince showed in his speech what his own party would say was good sportsmanship, and he built up that sportsmanship because, when his party had reviled and neglected us, he reviled not again during his speech, except to say one thing-and I quote what he said:
It is difficult to estimate just how much Prince Edward Island suffered during that period.
[Mr. Quelch.J
No doubt the hon. member meant the delay in transportation and delay in getting our new ferry boat.
I desire also to congratulate the seconder, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cournoyer), on the excellence of his maiden speech. He likewise did his party full justice re the speech from the throne. Despite the fact that he resides in that great shipbuilding centre of Sorel, where our car ferry has been in the course of construction for the past number of years, we shall not hold him responsible for the many unfulfilled promises of her early completion by his government.
It is a year, Mr. Speaker, since the opening of the second session and we are now in the third. During that time, death has claimed three members of this house. In stature, charm and loyalty they were real, typical Canadians. In cheerfulness, accomplishment and geniality they were typical parliamentarians of this house. They may not be missed, since their seats will be filled, but I can say that they will be long remembered. During that time also, one gentleman from this side resigned his seat, and when I say "gentleman" everyone knows whom I mean. I refer to the Hon. Doctor Bruce.
The government then called elections to fill the vacancies, and I am now pleased to congratulate the winners and also to congratulate this side of the house on securing two or three most capable members.
The speech from the throne admits of varied forms of debate, its longitude being forty minutes and its latitude any distance or any subject of interest which the speaker or the constituency which he represents may desire to select. The speech from the throne is a governmental document prepared by the * cabinet and placed in the hands of His Excellency by his constitutional advisers; therefore any criticism of mine or any other member does not reflect in any way upon His Excellency the Governor General either in person or with regard to public affairs.
The speech from the throne, with its contents, is a programme, I might say, of indefinite policies and contains many speculations on what legislation may come before this house, but it is entirely void of any practical policy for the benefit of our country.
I wish to refer for a moment to some distinguished visitors who came to our province last summer. First of all, I would mention His Excellency the Governor General and Her Excellency the Viscountess Alexander of Tunis. Our province and people gave them a real welcome, only such as can be extended by that province, the garden of the gulf, and our

2Vie Address-Mr. McLure
veterans were pleased to add greatly to the celebration and the welcome they gave their soldier leader. Our idea in welcoming them was that they would return soon and visit us at greater length. That was our hope.
Another visitor I wish to mention-and we had a most pleasant visit from him-was the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), accompanied by his excellent lady Madame Chevrier.
I am sure they were pleased with the honour and reception that our people extended to them. Then came the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges) and some of his officials. We accorded them a real welcome- a maritime welcome to a maritimer. After that, we had the royal commission on Indian affairs, the chairman being the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown). He was accompanied by quite a number of members of the commission and their wives. While the Minister of Transport was in our province, he spoke to a large meeting of the Rotary club. His address was a smooth, idealistic speech, well delivered, on the subject of transportation. It was good study propaganda not only for his own department-

speechtext:
Thank you. Mr. Speaker.
I was saying, with reference to the speech delivered by the Minister of Transport, that it was good study propaganda for his department and government. Perhaps some of us, particularly myself, would rather have had him get down to the real problem of transportation as it affected our province. However we were glad to welcome him and regretted that his stay was so short, but he left us with the promise that he rvould come in another season without any time limit.
The Minister of Fisheries visited different parts of our province and spoke to the fishermen in the different localities he visited, and I must say that he dealt with the problems and the future of our fishing industry with a good deal of satisfaction to fishermen and others who listened to him. I am sorry the Minister of Fisheries is not in his seat at the moment, but I believe he made a little bit of ministerial departure when he spoke to a Liberal club in Prince county on the subject of Liberalism. The press was present, and the next day the paper that covers the island like the dew had an extended report of it. Whether these speeches of the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Fisheries were well timed 83166-791
for the benefit of the Summerside provincial by-election or not I do not know, but I do know that the Progressive Conservative candidate won. The Canadian National railway official, the Liberal candidate, was derailed, whil* the high school teacher came through with a win. I should like to refer to just one matter in connection with this provincial by-election and it is this. Up to the time this election was brought on, there was a shortage of refrigerator cars in connection with shipping but the Canadian National Railways, through somebody, had a surplus of those cars in Summerside and west, even to the discrimination of many other shipping points.
The royal commission on Indian affairs came at a time when they enjoyed real autumn weather. This commission visited the chief points which they were called upon to visit, but made an extended visit to Lennox island, the chief Indian reserve in our province. No doubt this commission will be making an interim report to the department, if they have not already done so. I hope that they looked carefully into the matter with the Indian chief at Lennox island brought before them, namely, political patronage with regard to government supplies for Indians. The complaint of the Indian chief, as given, was that when a permit was given for supplies the Indians were supposed to go to some government party store and buy what they wanted. There may be nothing wrong with that but, as the chief stated at the meeting of the commission, the Indians could not even get an itemized account. Surely it would be better if, when they are given their permit for supplies, they were allowed to go out and buy in whatever market they wish up to the full amount of their permit. I mention this only on behalf of those Indians who are getting those permits. It would make them seem more independent if they did not have to go to the government party stores to have the permit filled.
I would possibly be remiss in my duty, Mr. Speaker, if, in going over the distinguished visitors, I omitted the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and his visit to Prince Edward Island. He came on a factfinding visit with reference to the tourist business and our transportation. I might say that nobody is more welcome to our province than is the hon. member for Davenport; and the last words which were shouted out to him when he was leaving the meeting, as he was on his way to the Borden ferry, were, "We hope you will come again, John R."
In the course of a great many of the debates which we hear in this house, and outside it as well, speakers emphasize the matter of unity.
The Address-Mr. McLure

Let me say that the unity of Canada is only as strong as the fulfilment of the terms of confederation. I believe in confederation. It has made some success; but how much greater would be that success if this young nation and each of its provinces could have the fulfilment of the terms of confederation. We seem to be drifting farther away from unity as the government legislates. We find the government seeking now, as they have been for the last six months, to set up centralization of government for Canada. This government has claimed the right to amend the British North America Act without the consent of the electors in the respective legislatures of the various provinces. What does that mean? It means that, if this government can do that, there is a certain amount of confidence lost in our confederation pact. The objective and aim of the fathers of confederation was for a united British North American nation, our Canada. But this objective and aim cannot be attained when the terms of union remain unfulfilled and ignored by this government, thus retarding progress and development, in particular with regard to my province.
I shall now come to a particular subject of my own which I have discussed before in this house on several occasions, namely, the truck freight rates on the Borden-Tormentine ferry. In dealing with this matter I do not wish to be misunderstood, because I want to be absolutely fair with regard to it. Last year I was accused of unfair criticism with respect to this transportation problem. However, it is all a matter of what we consider to be the meaning of the word "criticism". This was well defined by a soldier in the great war when he said, "I believe that the only practical thing one can do when a mistake is made is to take a crack at the man who made it." Then he summarized it all by stating a very simple, effective and concise maxim, "Scratch where it itches." The thing that itches us down home in our province is our transportation situation and the heavy and exorbitant freight rates on the ferry. On previous occasions I have endeavoured to deal with the unjust, discriminating truck freight rate on the Borden-Tormentine ferry; but now, in view of the findings of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada tabled a few days ago, I certainly regret to read in the press across Canada, after the board rendered its judgment, headlines as follows: "Board ignores confederation pact entirely." On February 10, 1947, the Minister of Transport answered a question asked, as he stated, "by the junior member for Queens", 
regarding Borden-Tormentine freight truck rates, stating that the judgment of the board of transport commissioners had been rendered and would be printed for distribution immediately. Just to remind the house, this was a case of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada holding a sitting on July 17 and 18 last at Charlottetown with respect to Canadian National freight rates on the Borden ferry. It must have been a very difficult decision to render, because the judgment took over two hundred days to be rendered and brought to this house. If the judgment is as long as the time it has taken, I am afraid it will be beyond my powers to peruse it. However there is one unique feature in connection with the rendering of this judgment: it seemed to be synchronized with the very day I asked my question. Strange, Mr. Speaker, that great minds had one common thought in view.
While I have not been favoured with a printed copy of the findings so that I may study them, the press has given their main features. What do we find? The Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada ignore the confederation pact by which we entered confederation, and in doing so they have rendered a judgment. However, to their credit let me say this one thing, that they made the implied admission that it was beyond their jurisdiction to consider the Borden-Tormentine ferry freight rates as part of the agreement between Prince Edward Island and the Dominion of Canada.
I protested the holding of the board meeting when it was held on July 17 last, on the ground that they had no jurisdiction. And I protest again at their findings because they are not in accordance with and under the terms of the confederation agreement of 1873. I have no quarrel at this time with the Canadian National - Railways. They are the subcontractors operating under a government mandate. I am quite sure that from their point of view the railway company has done its work well in the past winter with regard to freight. During all this winter, freight has been very heavy indeed. They have only one boat with a capacity of ten cars to take care of the great amount of freight involved. I might say that for the shipment of potatoes for British account it will require 3.000 cars, or 1,500 cars each way. In addition to this, freight is piling up, such as feeds, fertilizers, fuels, and the like, which have to be carried over.
The work of the Canadian National Railways has been good, and, as I said, I have no quarrel with them. They worked hard this winter, and did their best to carry the freight

__________ The Address-Mr. McLure
The railway men "who operate their trains are excellent men, who operate under the skilful guidance of their superintendent, Mr. Montgomery. However I can readily understand that the Canadian National Railways have no interest in the welfare of our province and the transportation problem involved in the Borden-Tormentine ferry. They are in business for themselves; therefore I am not basing my claim or lodging my charges against them.
Let me cite two cases to show that they are interested only in the Canadian National Railways. When the late Sir Henry Thornton, one-time president of the Canadian National Railways, and some of his officials, were giving evidence before the Andrew Rae Duncan commission at Charlottetown in 1926, what do we find was his attitude at that time? In his evidence the president stated that the Canadian National Railways were not concerned with the terms of confederation, but they were just given a mandate from the government solely to operate the ferry.
Then again, on October 24, 1945, before a meeting of the standing committee on railways and shipping we find a similar statement made by the president of the railways. At that time President Vaughan was being asked a number of questions by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman), and one of his questions was this:
Are the rates on the ferry high, and does the C.N.R. set them?	"
This is the reply given by the president of the railways:
We do not think the rates are unusually high. Of course everything that goes over on the ferry is in direct competition with the railway. We think we are generous in allowing the trucks to go on the ferry at all.
Let me repeat the last sentence, "We think we are generous in allowing the trucks to go on the ferry at all." That is the statement which came from the president of the railways, that they do not own, do not charter or do not maintain that ferry. Hon. members can now judge just how much interest they have in transportation rates on the Borden-Tormentine ferry.	.
In 1926 the Duncan commission, in its findings with respect to the cost of operation, stated that the car ferry accounting should be taken out of the hands of the Canadian National Railways, and the cost of operation should be charged to the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. The reason given for this recommendation was that it was working an injustice against Prince Edward Island.
I am sure hon. members will agree that this is conclusive evidence that the railway company should not be allowed to set the freight rates cost for the truck traffic transportation on the car ferry system, as they do today. Time does not permit my dealing fully with this question. Therefore I shall summarize a few of the points I have emphasized.
We entered the union in 1873. The terms of union with respect to transportation were as follows:
That the dominion government shall assume and defray all the charges for the following services, viz:-
Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers, to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the dominion;
And such other charges as may be incident to, jmd connected with, the services which by the 'British North America Act, 1867," appertain to to general government, and as are or may be allowed to the other provinces.
From 1873 to 1915 Prince Edward Island dealt with dominion governments and pleaded with them for the fulfilment of the terms, but to practically no avail. Then in 1915 the Borden government of that day inaugurated the Borden-Tormentine system, which was a beginning toward implementing the transportation agreement. Then the operation of the Borden-Tormentine ferry was turned over to the C.N.R., and the federal government was to pay all deficits in connection with the operation. In 1919, when our mode of traffic changed with the advent of motor cars and motor trucks, our real problems showed up. Arbitrary rates were set for conveying motor cars and trucks. The charges for conveying motor cars for a return trip was $7, plus sixty cents for each passenger, and this for a distance of eighteen miles. In 1931, when the late R. J. Manion was minister of railways and canals, the Prince Edward Island government appealed to him and he reduced the rate from $7 to 83 without any board of transport commissioners being called in to adjudicate. He dealt directly, as was his right to do, with the government of Prince Edward Island.
I should like to mention a few of the prohibitive rates. I am not going into detail because I put these on the record before. A five-ton truck load of first-class commodities cost $60.65 for the return trip; for second-class commodities the rate is $54.65; for third-class, $50.65, and for fourth-class, $44.65. Those are prohibitive rates. A truck driver told me one day that, if he bought a new truck and made a trip a day, at the end of the month the Canadian National Railways would own the truck as well as himself.
The Address-Mr. McLure

In 1945 the matter of setting rates for the Borden-Tormentine ferry was placed before this house, and at that time the house was informed by the Minister of Transport, as reported on page 3685 of Hansard of 1945, that the Minister of Transport could not set the rate; this in spite of the fact that the former minister of railways and canals had reduced the rates by sixty per cent.
Let me refer again to the board of transport commissioners. They sat in Charlottetown on July 17 and 18 last and there listened to the evidence and rendered their decision. That verdict was not in accordance with the terms of confederation. Under the British North America Act the dominion parliament, and it alone, through the Minister of Transport of the government in power, has the exclusive authority over all matters such as rates, et cetera, on ferries between a province and any British or foreign country. I made my protest on those two points.
Such ferries should be treated as national highways under the pact of 1873. There is nothing in the Railway Act which gives the board of transport commissioners jurisdiction to determine rates, charges, et cetera on an interprovincial ferry which the railway does not own, does not charter or does not maintain. I am not going to take up much more of your time, Mr. Speaker, but in conclusion I wish to say that when we entered confederation in 1873 the aim of all parties to that contract of agreement was that there should be no barrier to interprovincial trade simply because my province of Prince Edward Island was an island.
I claim that the water route from Borden to Tormentine, a distance of nine miles, should be in effect a national highway. If there is to be a charge at all it should be based on the normal cost of moving freight over an equivalent mileage on land. This should be done without waiting for the completion of the new ferry. Both leaders of the two major parties agree with me. In 1941 the Hon. Charles A. Dunning, who represented Queens county, spoke there on our transportation problems. No doubt speaking with the authority of his leader, he said:	"It is in the bond of agreement
and it must be fulfilled." My leader on this side of the house agrees with that, because he has said:	"We believe that the water
route from Borden to Cape Tormentine should be in effect a national highway and must be treated as such."
Is it any wonder that we are dissatisfied with the shameful betrayal of our island's interests by the powers that be at Ottawa? Again I charge this government with gross

indifference and negligence in dealing with our ferry transportation problem. I shall give the house more of this a little later.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do so because this debate affords an opportunity to hon. members who may feel so disposed to bring to the attention of the government matters of particular interest to their constituents as well as matters concerning the nation as a whole. I shall be brief, for all that I desire to do at this stage of the debate is to lend support to my colleagues who have so ably defended the needs of agriculture and labour, as well as the interests of our veterans and senior citizens, and to place before the government matters which concern my own constituency.
I should like to call to the attention of the Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) that the citizens of Prince Albert constituency have waited too long for the promised improvements in our postal facilities in the city and the territory surrounding it. In an area as large as most constituencies across Canada, with a population of nearly 47,000, there is not one rural free delivery route in the constituency. The postal facilities for the city itself are not what they should be for a city the size of Prince Albert and the territory it serves. Then again, all those who are so faithful in seeing that the mail gets through in all kinds of weather; in our city and from the railway points to inland post offices, whether in the offices or delivering, are paid far too little for the arduous tasks they perform. Especially those couriers who, through all kinds of weather, carry the mail from railway points to inland post offices. They, too, should come under the bonus arrangements provided for by this house and, when the Postmaster General's estimates are before us, we shall continue to press this matter further.
I should also like, Mr. Speaker, through you to call to the attention of the Minister of Transport the petition from the citizens of the city of Prince Albert to the Canadian National for a new railway station. The present building is entirely inadequate in every way. It does not meet the need of the railways themselves, particularly the government-owned railway, for efficient and proper handling of the passenger and express service of the city and the vast territory surrounding it, particularly to the north and west. The petition sets forth clearly and precisely the need and furnishes the statistical data which proves conclusively the immediate need of such an undertaking on the part of our government owned railway.

The Address-Mr. Bowerman
I would urge the Minister of Transport to give the matter his careful and considerate attention.
Then there is the matter of the Prince Albert national park, one of the most beautiful of nature's playgrounds in all Canada. We in Saskatchewan and the north central part in particular, feel that the government has failed to provide the means for developing the park to the extent that should have been done. There was perhaps good reason for this during the war years. But now that is behind us and we are looking toward the future. Thousands more Americans from the middle western states would spend their vacations at the park were roads and park facilities such as they should and very well could be. Money spent along these lines wouldi pay not only dividends in good United States money, but dividends beyond measure in neighbourly good will and understanding that cannot be measured in dollars and cents. I hope that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) will keep this matter in mind, for we hope to deal more in detail with it when his estimates are in committee.
I should also like to say in passing that Prince Albert is still waiting for the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) to fulfil the promise which he made regarding runways for the airport when he was in the -city prior to the last election.
There is another more urgent and pressing matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the government, particularly the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), who are not in their seats at the moment. It has to do with the vocational school in Prince Albert. I have discussed the matter with the Minister of Labour and I am hoping that he and his colleagues will reconsider their decision to close this school on April 15. In letters just received from the president of the student council of the school and a prominent member of the city council, they ask that the government give these pre-matriculation students, fourteen in number, all of whom are veterans, a better break. They feel that the psychological effect of change of domicile from one city to another 110 miles distant, with the fear of unsuitable housing accommodation being found, the change of instructors, adapting themselves to new surroundings, with their examinations or tests only two months away, is disturbing, to say the least, and might easily result in their failing to pass their examinations. I believe that these veterans and their families have earned the right to better treatment. The government can well afford, in
view of the small cost, to continue this school until the expiration of the term in June. Surely the government can at least be as generous as the instructors who, I am informed, have offered to continue to teach without salary in order that these men, the pick of this school, may have every opportunity to finish without hindrance to their studies. Mr. Speaker, through you, I again urge the ministers concerned to continue this school until the end of June when the veterans will have completed their studies and finished their tests.
