speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking in the house last session I put on record that I was in favour of increased pensions for persons over sixty years of age. I also stated that there should be a contributory pension plan. If each Canadian desiring this type of pension were to contribute one dollar a month from the age of twenty-one, or $12 a year, at the age of sixty he would have contributed $468, and if the government duplicated these payments the amount would be $936. If the man or woman lived to the age of sixty and kept up the payments, with the government contributions, they would amount to $1,785.62; and at sixty-five years of age the fund would amount to $1,906.47. The contributor should then receive $50 a month without any means test.
We must remember that our people to whom the government would start to pay these annuities were born in the seventies and eighties of the last century. Many of them started to build their homes around 1900 to 1910. They struggled to build their homes and rear their families through some trying periods. Surely, in view of the great development of her resources, Canada will not continue to allow her people to suffer want or hardship as they come to the eventide of life. These people have helped to make Canada what she is today, a great and prosperous country. In this connection I wish to put on record an item from the Guelph Mercury, one of the leading papers in western Ontario. It says:
A'ears ago old age pensions wrere looked upon as the rankest kind of socialism. The view of many persons, was that every man should provide for his old age or suffer the inevitable consequences.
In this enlightened age, however, it is recognized that many factors enter into success or failure and that the most well-intentioned person in the world may suffer reverses that will leave him. in the autumn of life, with not enough funds for actual existence, and the same set of circumstances holds true, of course, for women.
It may he argued, of course, that the old age pensions set something of a premium on carelessness, and might have the effect of making
The Address-Mr. Menary

many persons less anxious to provide tor their idle years. Perhaps in some eases this will be found true. It would not be sufficient reason to refrain from continuing and increasing this payment of such first rate importance to a large number of deserving people.
According to statistics, the life expectancy of every Canadian is a little over sixty-four years, and it is said that the number of persons in the United States who are over sixty-five years is growing year by year. Even if our average expectancy of life exceeds that of any other people, it falls far short of what we have a right to expect. It is generally accepted that the life span of any animal should be approximately five times the length of the period required to reach maturity. A horse, for instance, matures at five years of age and lives to about twenty-five. A man should live to 100 years of age, if he is well looked after and is free from worries when he is sixty. There is considerable evidence to support the conclusion that man should live a healthy and active life until he is 100 years old, but the confusion, competition, disappointment, and unhealthful factors in their surroundings have made many city dwellers old at the age of fifty. We have good reason to believe that the average resident of our rural districts lives to a greater age than the average city dweller, but we are living in an industrial era. Science has not yet succeeded in guaranteeing good health into the old age of any of our citizens and, until this is achieved we, the members of this parliament, must not shirk our duty. We must adequately provide for all those Canadians no longer able to care for themselves.
In spite of the time that has elapsed since the end of the war, many urgent problems of our veterans remain unsolved. Many of them are finding it difficult to establish themselves in civilian life. In my riding hundreds of men have come back from the armed forces. Some have gone into farming, others into industry and business. I wish to mention three cases. A young lad of eighteen went overseas. He was a butcher, and when he came back he started in the butcher business again. He found it hard to get meat from the packers, and he could not secure a slaughtering permit. Our friends of the wartime prices and trade board said that he did not qualify for a slaughtering permit. He wrote to me to see if I could help him. I took the matter up with the wartime prices and trade board and they listed the various things which the young man could not get. This young man had a wife and they were both trying to establish a home. One day I dropped in to see him and he was very much discouraged. I asked him how much meat he had had 
lately and he replied that during the last three weeks he had had one-quarter of beef-one-quarter of beef to run a butcher shop. He said that the hospital rang up one morning and wanted 10 or 15-pound roasts. He said that if he had sold them what they wanted he would have had very little left for his other customers. It seems to me that these regulations are making it difficult for our young men to get a decent start in life.
Two other young men in my riding returned from overseas and tried to start an electrical wiring business. They met the same problem, no quota. They had not been in business before. They were helped out through the kindness of a hardware merchant who, since he had been in business for a long time, was able to get some material, although not half enough to keep these two boys going.
Another young man who spent five years in the air force purchased a retail lumber yard in my riding. He informs me that he can get plenty of work, but on account of the various controls the necessary lumber cannot be obtained. Everyone knows that a black market exists in lumber. If controls are taken off, prices may rise but not for long, because the public are shopping around. There is not the wild scramble that took place in war years. The lifting of controls is necessary to help our trade, and it will reroute lumber into legitimate channels. Only by taking off these controls can we help the thousands of returned boys who are finding that even if they purchase a business they are held in straitjackets by controls administered by a lot of bureaucrats who probably would not hold their positions had they been able to run a business of their own.
Various housing schemes have been mentioned in this chamber. I come from a small town of about nine hundred to one thousand people. When I hear speakers mention houses of 88,000, $9,000 or $10,000 I can hardly see the picture at all. Just before I came here I was talking to a merchant. I said: "Clarence, when are you going to move into your house?" He said, "Oh, in about two weeks." I said, "What did it cost you, Clarence?" He has a beautiful little house; it has a cement cellar under all of it, a bathroom with all the necessary fixtures, hardwood floors, and it is built of dressed lumber. It has two rooms upstairs and three downstairs. He said it cost him $4,500. When I hear of the poor soldiers paying $6,000 or $7,000 for a house I do not see how they are going to do so. There is another house up the street built by a Mr. Geer. He has been living in it for about two

The Address-Mr. Hlynka
months. I understand that it cost him around $4,500, and it is a splendid little house. I was in it and it-is well finished inside.
I wish to join with hon. members on this side of the house in support of the stand that all controls, except that of rent, should be abolished. They have become irksome to the people of Canada. All our citizens were willing to help in all ways to win the struggle which engulfed our country in 1939, but now the war is over and we wish to return to private enterprise. Controllers quite often find themselves leaning toward dictatorship and the longer these controls continue, the closer we will approach this form of government which, I am sure, is undesirable to the majority of Canadians.

In the course of the present debate several hon. members on both sides of the house have placed their stand on record on the question of freight rates now being heard by the board of transport commissioners. I should like also to take this opportunity to make clear the position of the Social Credit group on this important question, and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I shall not transgress the rules of the house.
In the Alberta brief on dominion-provincial relations entitled, "The Case for Alberta" issued in 1938, the social crediters have stated their position clearly on the question of freight rates as recorded on pages 142 to 178 inclusive. In the thirty-six pages devoted to the discussion of freight rates many examples of inequities under which the prairie provinces have suffered are cited. It is pointed out, for example, that the people of Alberta are paying the highest freight charges of any province on goods exported from other provinces, and on practically all incoming goods. This results in an addition to the cost of production, which addition is not recovered in the price the farmer receives from the sale of his products, thereby diminishing his income, It also results in a smaller return to the farmer.
Recognizing this discrimination against the western provinces, "The Case for Alberta" recommended equalization and a downward revision of freight rates structure. That, Mr. Speaker, remains the position which members of the Social Credit group take. In other words this group will keep on pressing for equalization and complete overhauling of the freight rates structure in Canada. However we are also not unmindful of the fact that it is in the interest of our national economy to have smoothly and efficiently running railways. If it can be shown that it is absolutely necessary for the railways to have additional
revenue to operate efficiently we would not object to any justifiable adjustment, but definitely not at the expense of the prairie provinces or of any one part of Canada. The load should be borne equally by the whole nation.
To determine the financial position of the railways we would urge that a royal commission be appointed, on which western agriculture should be given representation, and that the problem be studied and reported back to this parliament. It would be up to the government and to the railways to supply the house with accurate figures as to the earnings and operation costs to enable members of parliament to vote intelligently. Failing this, the Social Credit group will oppose any upward revision of the freight rates structure and will continue to press for a downward revision and equalization of freight rates for the entire country.

speechtext:
In taking part in this debate I do so with a great deal of interest as a lumberman and on behalf of my constituents. Like practically every other hon. member, I have received many letters and telegrams on the decontrol of various products, especially lumber. In doing so, I am at the same time taking the chance of putting my own business in the bad graces of the control bureaucracy, because it is well understood that the department can make it very miserable for anyone in the lumber business if they so desire. However I shall confine my few remarks mainly to timber control. Timber control has become the home of the greatest swivel-chair bureaucracy of all times. They are becoming red-tape specialists. They have added more rigid control in the past year than we had during the whole time of the war period.
As regards control experts, somebody has defined an expert as one who is seldom right but never in doubt. I suggest that a good definition would probably be that they are just ordinary people away from home. At any rate, they set up a price of approximately $40 for hemlock. Now, anyone who knows anything about lumbering will realize that hemlock cannot be produced in Ontario or Quebec for that price. The net result has been, first, that lumbermen have been forced on the black market in different respects, and, second, that they leave their stands of hemlock and work in other species out of which they can make some profit. Therefore hemlock which is needed so badly for housing, is not being taken out. The lumbermen of today are sound business people, very few of them being fly-by-night opportunists.
The Address-Mr. Hodgson

As far as exports are concerned, I believe the government has to allow the exporting of lumber to some degree, I would say about forty per cent, because in the eastern part of Canada you have lumbering that depends on the export trade, as the freight haul to central Canada is too great compared with the distance to the ocean and the United States. The same applies to western Canada, British Columbia in particular.
Central Canada does get and use some British Columbia lumber, gjenerally large and long square timber at large and long prices, or the low end, which they have a surplus of and can afford to sell at cheaper prices.
Then for Ontario and Quebec, exportation is mostly of selects, first and seconds in the heavier stock of hardwoods, which has always been in the export trade and not used to any great extent in Canada, and definitely not in housing. No. 2 and 3 com. hardwood is used in the manufacture of flooring.
I say, therefore, that the exporting of lumber does not affect our housing schemes to the degree for which it gets credit. The whole question of housing, or any other industry for that matter, is production. Therefore, if encouragement can be given to the lumber industry to produce, and a feeling of good will established, rather than the sour, disgruntled taste which is in every lumberman's mind against controls, that encouragement should be given, because lumbermen feel that, since they stayed with the ship through the war, they should now have some relief.
In my constituency there are veterans and others who have gone to the bush to take out logs, but now they find that they cannot get nails and other necessary materials with which to build homes. There are no supplies in the country. In fact, there is not a storekeeper in the country who has a nail to sell. While the war was on, we put up with controls and did our best to produce lumber under those conditions. Now that the war has been over for two years, there is not the same patriotic feeling prevailing among producers. In my riding there are five mills that are not taking out lumber this year and this will mean a difference of five million feet in one riding alone. If the same thing happens throughout Canada there will be a considerable falling off in production, running into hundreds of millions of feet.
Two lumbermen from my constituency have gone south for the winter. One, who is in Texas, wrote to me a few days ago and said that roping steers in Texas is a lot more fun than roping logs in four feet of snow and 
thirty degrees below zero. The other is in California. He said he was going to start picking oranges and would probably make enough in that way to pay his trip expenses.
The less efficiency there is, the more controls are added. For instance, if a lumberman wants to sell lumber to one of his old reliable customers or anyone else, he must submit four copies of the order to the timber controller's office for approval and authorization. Then, as each car goes forward, he must send a copy of each invoice for each car to the timber controller's office. They reserve the right to inspect these cars at destination or anywhere en route. Quite often a car is held for several days waiting for the inspector to arrive, and when he does finally get there, the chances are he knows very little about the grading or inspection of hardwood lumber, for out of every ten inspectors who were put on this job there were about two who could qualify to grade lumber.
Timber control was first inaugurated in 1940 and price control came in eighteen months later. H. R. MacMillan was the first controller. He knew the lumber industry and he got around him men who knew their jobs. True, he was a dollar a year man and he stayed only one year. In a little over six years of timber control there have been seven controllers. Only two of these knew anything about the lumber business: MacMillan and Nicholson. The last one or the immediate past one, was a hotelkeeper; then he practised law and then became a soldier. He was married to a well known politician's daughter, rapidly rose in the service, and became timber controller.
Since the war, the employees MacMillan brought into the timber control have mostly gone back to their bid jobs, and today we have an organization operating that has only one employee who knows or ever had anything to do with the lumber industry. I ask the minister to name one, except this old gentleman in the person of Malcolm MacNickoI, who did have something to do with a small retail business, but his experience was only in one phase of the industry and his outlook is limited.
All the outstandingly able assistants have retired, and the persons replacing them are men not overly confident of their ability to compete in industry and who would rather keep their hand on the doorknob of some patronage job.
When timber control came in as a war measure the government passed orders in council to ensure that controls would be free from political interference, influence or dicta-

The Address-Mr. Hodgson
tion, and each control immediately set up machinery for consultation with industry. Now with the close of hostilities, two years past, with the emergency of war forgotten, what have we? A general admission that decisions on matters of control are matters of political policy.
The decision as to whether or not control should come off lumber is not a question of whether or not it is to the interest of the lumber industry, but rather how it will affect votes. An analysis of these facts will give the answer to why controls are failing and will continue to fail. They have outlived their usefulness, and their continuance is a menace to the success of the whole lumbering economy as well as a handicap to other industries dependent on lumber supply. The lumber industry has no say in and no responsibility toward a control policy, and there is a condition of chaos and frustration developing, which can be corrected only by abolishing control and a return to unhampered free trading.
The lumbering business is a basic one, which holds a top-ranking position in the Canadian economy. Rather than that being the reason why decontrol of this great industry cannot be judged on its merits, it is all the more reason why forest products should be freed from restrictions which are hampering its activities.
Surely the industry has first-hand knowledge of the harm which the continuation of controls is working, and can judge the effects which the elimination of controls would have. The war is over; the justification of control regulations no longer exists, and the quicker obstacles to the normal lumber trade are removed, the better. Wage controls have disappeared and food prices have increased. The very fact that the industry is unanimous for decontrol should be sufficient. At the Canadian lumbermen's convention held in Montreal on February 10, 11 and 12-the largest group of lumbermen ever assembled in Canada- they met in separate groups representing six different organizations of the lumbering industry, which included bush and sawmill operators, retail and wholesale dealers and so on. They voted in separate groups for the removal of controls and in the general meeting they were unanimous to have controls removed at once, there being not one dissenting vote out of over fifteen hundred delegates. Can the government honestly believe that such a bureaucracy as has been set up in Ottawa can run all the lumber industry in Canada better than the lumbermen themselves? I am convinced that, unless controls are removed immediately, there is now and will be further
decreases in the production of lumber. This will cause a decrease in employment in the industry itself and in every other industry depending upon a supply of lumber. Certainly, viewed from a sound business or economic point of view, the prompt withdrawal of controls would be a sound and logical move. I put some questions on the order paper on February 13, but they have not yet been answered so that I cannot tell what the cost of controls is.
I know, however, that it runs into a great deal of money that is unnecessarily spent.
I wish to say a word now on taxation of soft drinks. The soft drinks industry collects forty per cent, or two cents a bottle, and pays it to the dominion treasury. It does not help the industry and, moreover, the soft drinks are paid for mostly by children. The hon. member for London said that the baby bonus was given to help the children to buy soft drinks, but he added that it was like giving a child ten cents to go to bed and taking it away from him while he slept.
There is another aspect to this matter. While the war was on, our children were buying war savings stamps and they contributed a great deal of money to the war requirements at that time. I think it was a good thing because it created in the child a sense of patriotic duty. I know when the children came home with their first stamp they were pleased, and when they got enough for a certificate they were pleased and proud of it. Now, when they go to the store and have to pay that two cents extra on pop, I wonder if this government are helping the confidence of the children and that patriotic feeling? Are they not creating a feeling in the child's mind that he is paying for his own bond all over again with every bottle of pop that he consumes?

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate, but there have been certain information and criticism brought to my attention which I feel must be answered in order that the citizens of my own county may be protected. One department that has been severely criticized by many hon. members of the opposition during this debate is the Department of Veterans Affairs, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie), particularly with regard to veterans housing.
I have listened attentively to the debate, and the impression I get is that in their criticism hon. members have left with many of us on this side of the house the definite idea that contractors and those engaged in the
building trade in Ontario and western Canada should hang their heads in shame. It has amused me to see how cleverly an attempt has been made to place on the government's doorstep full responsibility for the condition of some veterans houses in western Canada and at the same time protect those directly responsible for this condition-the contractors themselves.
We in eastern Canada have had a shortage of building materials owing to the greatly increased demand, and in many cases it has been found necessary to make use of inferior materials in the building of veterans homes and those for civilian use as well. The home owner was fully aware of this condition, and I am convinced that in no way were these particular materials camouflaged in order to deceive the purchaser. Many veterans homes are under construction in the county of Charlotte and many have been completed. I feel confident that the contractors responsible for the erection of these homes were conscientious and that the welfare of the veteran received every consideration.
If the information disclosed during this debate relative to veterans housing is correct, deceit and fraud are evident in the building trade in western Canada and some hon. members of this house are endeavouring to camouflage the evidence, no doubt for political purposes, by placing full responsibility upon the government. If those directly responsible, that is the contractors, were dealt with as they should be the citizens would be apprised of those involved in this nefarious and shameful practice. By such action, not only would the veterans be protected but so would our entire population. I am pleased to state that in Charlotte county this condition does not exist, and in no way could those responsible for the building of veterans houses be associated with those engaged in a like occupation in western Canada.
We have on this side of the house a veteran of the last war who is directly connected with the building of veterans homes. If such accusations as have been made in this house were directed against the company with which he is associated they would not go by unanswered. Knowing him as I do, I can assure the house that he would not tolerate any man or any group of men who would take unfair advantage of any veteran.
In one breath hon. members opposite are saying that the government should reduce the personnel of departments in order to cut expenditures. Then suggestions are made to increase the staff by way of inspectors to watch over these big-hearted contractors in their own constituencies who are defrauding these young
The Address-Mr. Stuart

men who, as one member stated, went into the very jaws of death to protect you and me and have come back to receive nothing but lip service. That lip service is coming from some of the hon. members opposite wh o, during this entire debate, have been most critical, but who have made few suggestions of a constructive nature.
Unlike those engaged in the building trade in western Canada, the Minister of Veterans Affairs-I think all will agree with this-is very much interested in the welfare of thousands of returned veterans in every part of this great country. If he and his department received a little more cooperation from hon. members, instead of criticism which is not of a constructive nature, it would be of great benefit to the war veterans and would save much time in this chamber. In no way do I wish to criticize those responsible for the decision made to repair veterans homes at the expense of the taxpayers. The veteran should never be obliged to replace faulty materials or correct defects of any kind.
However, if it is found that the contractor is legally responsible, irrespective of the type of contract, be it cost-plus or management fee, he should be held accountable for all defects. Under contracts of this kind he is protected from loss in every way and the Canadian public should be given the same protection. Under such contracts it is not excusable that faulty workmanship should be found, especially if the contractors have the interests of the war veterans in their hearts. Six or seven hundred thousand dollars is a lot of money for the public to furnish to cover up blunders and defects which apparently are evident in the construction of veterans homes in certain parts of this country. I regret that such a situation does exist. I regret also that citizens of this country are associated with such a scandal. Men of this type are not good citizens, and I have little regard for any person who would deliberately and ill-advisedly wrong, cheat or defraud a veteran of this dominion who has given so much for which we should all be thankful. In many cases the particular veteran may have left a brother on the other side.
When the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) was speaking on this subject he gave the name of a construction company responsible for housing conditions in his riding, and he had this to say, as reported on page 108 of Hansard:
I regret to say to this house that my friends built these houses, and I feel very badly because I must stand up here and tell the house and the people of Canada of such home construction for veterans. But if I am to be entitled to be elected to represent my constituency, or any

other hon. members are entitled to be elected, our duty to our country comes before our duty to our friends.
I congratulate the hon. member for Lambton West upon his outspoken statement. If detailed information were given in every case the publicity might be responsible for a great improvement in the housing situation. I disagree with only one portion of his statement. The hon. member stated that his friends had built these houses. I would hesitate to say that men responsible for defrauding the war veterans of this country were my friends. If they will take advantage of a veteran, what chance has a civilian?
In conclusion, may I say that we have very little in the maritime provinces that people in central and western Canada can make use of. We have always been obliged to look elsewhere for our export markets, but in this particular case, if it is impossible to find honest men in the construction business in this part of Canada, or honest inspectors, come down to the maritimes. I assure you that that type of man can be found there. True to maritime tradition we are always ready and willing to give a helping hand.

speechtext: I begin by congratulating the hon. member for Saint Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Hamel) and by seconding the motion which stands in his name on the order paper, requesting that the Labour-Progressive party be outlawed in this country. These are worth-while measures which we should all support. There are hon. members and Canadian newspapermen who have deemed fit to spill ink over the motion which stands in my name on the order paper and who have written insolently about it; the resolution, so they claim, is Utopian, senseless.

Mr. Speaker, instead of speaking of the amount of money that such a programme would entail for the country, the government and hon. members should ask themselves whether it would be possible to produce sufficiently to implement such a programme.
We must take into account Canada's potentialities and distribute with logic and intelligence the corresponding amount of money to

Canadian consumers. Such is the nature of the motion I have placed on the order paper. I mean that we should give our money to Canadians before giving it to foreigners.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: If that is what you want, then it is all Greek.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Excellent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -as well as its provincial chairman and the member for Pontiac. Let us examine his speech and its implications.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The hon. member for Terrebonne intimated that a member of the Union of Electors was reluctant to divulge his identity, that he did not wish to say that he belonged to the Social Credit group. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am a representative of the Union of Electors in this house, and I am not afraid to say that I am one hundred per cent in favour of the Social Credit movement. I wish to make it clear that I am a supporter of the Social Credit philosophy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: At last, he has shed the mask.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Some people claim that the Social Credit members of parliament are imperialists, that they are warmongers; that has nothing to do with the Social Credit policies. If an English-speaking Catholic from Ontario is for conscription or if a Frenchspeaking Catholic from Quebec is against conscription, that has nothing to do whatever with the value of the Catholic religion. One could not say, for this reason, that the Catholic religion is objectionable in Canada. That has nothing to do with the doctrine itself. Well, we, members of the Social Credit group, have an economic doctrine, a logic and a philosophy which meet the aspirations of human beings; we suggest that money must be made the servant of man and not the reverse; we want as much money in circulation in peace time as there was in war time.
Everybody knows what the government did for this country in the last war; but now that the war is over, we want these things done for Canadian citizens.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You may question me to your heart's content after I am through.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would the hon. member say if he favours controls to permit equitable distribution of the money he mentions?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I favour an equitable distribution of such money as the country's production can supply.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
When you say that,
do you also mean that you favour controls to attain that end?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: For its wartime needs, the government did not wonder if there was enough money in Canada. It felt it should do everything that was physically possible in the way of providing armaments, guns, rifles, and uniforms. Everything that is physically possible for warfare must be made financially possible. And at no time during the war, Mr. Speaker, was the production of guns, or even of a single cartridge, ever hindered by a lack of money. Money was raised according to possibilities or rather to the necessity with which we were confronted to produce what was required for the destruction of mankind or the protection of our fellow citizens-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: By taxes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes. Since my honourable friend speaks of taxes, I should like to remind him that in 1939 the government could not raise any taxes because the people had no money. It was essential, first of all, to put money in the hands of the taxpayer. We all know how this was achieved. War was used as a means of distributing money to the taxpayer and then came taxes-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And loans also.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, and loans also.
Mr. Speaker, the honourable member for Terrebonne stated that the programme of the Union of Electors did not make sense and in order to prove that the people had no faith in it he quoted Le Droit of Ottawa and the Fronliere of Rouyn. If my honourable friend wishes to get information from people having no knowledge of its subject let him do so, let him consult people who have never made any study of our doctrine, but at the same time he will become the laughing stock of the whole province and that is only natural.
Let us ask ourselves if Canada can produce sufficiently to guarantee to the aged of 60 and over $60 a month; if Canada can produce sufficiently to guarantee our invalids $60 a
The Address-Mr. Caouette

month when they have reached the age of 21, and if Canada can produce sufficiently to guarantee each and every citizen decent means of livelihood. That is why we request a $20 monthly national dividend.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is not enough!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: This is where we have trouble making some people understand.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That's not surprising!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That a company should distribute to each of its shareholders at the end of the year, the percentage to which he is entitled in the profits earned, seems entirely logical. This is effected through dividends. That a credit union should distribute a dividend at the end of the year to each of its members, on the basis of his shares also seems quite in order. It is the thing to do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is the salary earned by capital.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Why admit that much? If everyone agrees, it must be right and well organized. Coordinated work alw'ays gives good results. Think, for instance, of the Noranda mine in my constituency. Some miners are working at 7,000 feet underground, others at 2,000 feet, others at the surface, or at the mill or in offices-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Others are in their second childhood.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And work is well
organized-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, sometimes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As it is well done and well organized, what happens at the end of the year? The mine brings profits, which is normal; however, the mine would not be as profitable if work were not well organized and every miner were continuously employed at 7,000 feet underground, and the mine owner would also be in the hole.
In society, Mr. Speaker, work is organized. The hon. members did not make the shoes that they are wearing; they were made by shoe manufacturers. They did not make the clothing that they are wearing; but they are clothed just the same. There are numerous social organizations. We have doctors, we have all kinds of other professional men; all work for the common good, for the general interests of society. Because work has been organized in an intelligent way in Canada there are surpluses at the end of the year. Because the work is organized intelligently, the production system is excellent in Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We have a good government too.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The production system suits us, because the organization is -well balanced. At the end of the year the production exceeds the existing purchasing power.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, production exceeds the existing purchasing power inasmuch as we can afford to ship goods to other countries. We have a surplus.
We then export our surplus, but the question is: To what use should we put it? The difference between a country's total production and total purchasing power must be balanced with new money, not money created by bankers but money created by a responsible government, a government that should be sovereign. And that surplus production must not be distributed the world over but among the people of Canada; it should be made available to everyone. It should be computed after deduction of salaries and profits. It is not a question of cutting out salaries or profits. The new currency should be based on the difference between total production and purchasing power, and it should be distributed among all Canadian citizens, the whole Canadian people, in the form of a national dividend. I feel that this is merely logical, Christian-like and even democratic. It affords the means to ensure freedom and security to all Canadians.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The dividend is not
high enough.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Eighty dollars!

speechtext:
It was stated in the house by the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand) that:
The resolution moved by the hon. member for Pontiac and the programme of the Union of Electors border on Utopia, and I might even say on election hysteria.
He stated a little farther on that the resolution appearing on the order paper was simply an electoral platform. That is exactly what I stated before the election. Hon. members will, however, own that it is very seldom that arguments uttered in the course of an electoral campaign are repeated in parliament. I do it. Before the election, the electors of my constituency had this very programme. They sent me here to promote it. I shall do

The Address-Mr. Caouette
it in spite of everyone. I shall demand what the electors of my constituency will ask me to place before parliament. It may happen that members opposite will ask what our programme is as the hon. member for Terrebonne has done. After having criticized the programme of the Union of Electors, he spoke of a very interesting matter:
The Social Credit party claim that their financial methods would settle the problem. Can people in their right senses be taken in by such statements? No. The people want old age pensions at an earlier age.
What difference is there between this demand and ours?
. . . old age pensions at an earlier age, allowances for the needy crippled and invalids, gradual reduction of taxes . . .
The hon. member wanted to know how our programme could be implemented while reducing taxes. It is by reducing them gradually, that he intends to implement his own programme:
. . . continued employment and fair working conditions, opportunity for ownership, in short, happiness within the framework of a sound and progressive economy.
Mr. Speaker, I believe the hon. member for Terrebonne will eventually occupy a seat on this side of the house.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No danger of that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Our programme tends to enhance everyone's happiness. Is it possible to know, in Canada, whether the country is in a position to produce goods for the Canadians? The heavy production of weapons, during the war, in our country, is a well-known fact. When the hon. member for Terrebonne stated that the Social Credit members were in favour of extending help to strangers, during the conflict, he was forgetting that, after the war, they wish to give money to the Canadians. That is a matter he has not mentioned. That is one thing which he has not yet been willing to admit. Mr. Speaker, Canada has increased her wealth during the past years.
The honourable member then spoke about the change in seasons; he has said the Social Credit changed with the seasons. I must say that it is rather the Liberal party and the Liberal policy that have undergone such a seasonal change during the last 25 years.
Mr. Speaker, we want Canada to be for Canadians. Hysteria or demagogy does not enter the picture. Demagogy comes from those who in the past have caused the people to suffer hardships. We do not want that, we want Canada to be for Canadians. Let us
consider history, and we shall see that all those who have tried to help the people have been branded as demagogues, or worse. As far as we are concerned, we shall carry on our work throughout the country, and in the near future, Mr. Speaker, we shall have in Canada a government responsible to the Canadian electors, a government which will promote their interests rather than be concerned with election funds.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The honourable member will kindly allow me to ask him just one question, because I am seeking information. If I am not mistaken he said a few moments ago that the government should make up for the lack of money through the issue of currency. Would he be willing to explain the machinery to be used in that connection and tell us whether that money circulated throughout the country would create debt?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That money would be absolutely debt-free, since it would be created by a sovereign government. Instead of asking bankers to issue money, or to produce it in the form of loans to the government, the state would itself create money based upon the actual wealth of the country. I mean that such money would correspond to that wealth.

May I ask a further
question?

The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette) is reproaching us for not studying social credit. I would like to know something about it but he does not want to answer my questions.

We have been telling
you about it for twelve years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the riding I represent is considered a rural constituency. The people who make up that riding are good people, a hard-working, industrious people. W7e have not been noted for becoming millionaires but we get along wonderfully well under the circumstances. Our largest town has a population below 3,000 most of the year, and an added population of summer visitors running into the thousands. My home town of Kincardine is holding its centennial celebration in 1948, and I assure you, sir, that you and any of the members of this house who can visit with us on that occasion will be welcomed and royally entertained, not only by the members of this house who were born in Bruce but also by the descendants of the early pioneers w'ho made our county one of

The Address-Mr. A. E. Robinson
the best counties in Ontario and also one of the best known counties throughout the western provinces.
It will be readily understood that in a rural riding like Bruce we have an active federation of agriculture. I have heard it said that the federation of agriculture is leaning toward socialism. Such is not the case in Bruce. I do not believe it is true of the top officials of the federation, and if the federation were leaning toward socialism it would surely defeat the object of the organization, which is to help out organized agriculture. What agriculture needs is not so much being helped out as to secure a square deal in comparison with other occupations in Canada. We have worked hard through the war years and have not received overpayment for the number of hours worked. At the present time there is not the inclination amongst young people to settle on the many vacant farms which we have. I am sure that if the farmers were getting a square deal financially there would be many of these young people who would settle on these vacant farms, and that in turn would go a long way toward relieving the acute housing shortage which this government seems unable to remedy. We know the conditions that prevail on the majority of farms. The owners are mostly elderly men who no longer have strength to carry on. They cannot get help. They cannot sell. The demand for farms is limited, and prices offered are generally lower than the value of the buildings, with nothing left for the land. They cannot rent, so they do the only thing left. They seed down the land and turn it to pasture, and the productivity is less than a quarter of what it might be. This condition prevails over most of Ontario. During the war the farmers did a wonderful and heroic job. With less help they produced a great deal more. They did it by working almost impossible hours. On Bruce farms the work week has averaged between eighty and ninety hours the year round, and no holidays. In summer, Sunday work has been from three to five hours; in winter, six to eight hours. Farm women, many of them with little families, with no help in the house, and too often without the conveniences that in towns are considered an everyday necessity, drove tractors, tended poultry, milked cows, helped with the haying and harvesting, and somehow found time besides for a good deal of social life. The average farmer is, I may say, not interested in an eight-hour day but more interested in an eight-hour night.
Such conditions are not good for the future welfare of Canada. There is talk of this gov-

ernment spending millions of dollars in opening up more farm lands in Canada. Would any government not be wise to try to make the present farmer's lot such that we could make 100 per cent use of the good land that is now available? Who ever heard of a merchant failing in business when surrounded with farmers who were flush with money, free from debt and adding a little each year to their bank accounts? Prosperity among farmers does not depend on crops altogether but on their having money in their pockets, and able to pay cash down for everything they need from town. The outlook for farming under the present government is not good, but I see a ray of hope from the fact that we, the official opposition, have as our leader the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Bracken), who understands farming from all angles. He has made a life study of it. He is eager and willing to fight for farmers' rights from the drop of the hat. I am predicting that our hon. leader will be the next Prime Minister of Canada. When that time comes, and may it be soon, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers of Canada will get their fair share of the national income.
Before this debate on the speech from the throne finishes, I wish to say a few words on decentralization. I shall avail myself of that opportunity at the present time. Decentralization is not only a big word, but also a big subject. It is a subject that is not receiving enough attention in Canada today. Nearly every move the present government has made has been toward centralization. During the war this government encouraged the building of large industries in the thickly populated areas. Most of those industries are peace-time industries at the present time. The government missed a wonderful chance by not placing many of these new factories among the smaller towns and villages; thereby the migration would not have been to the larger centres, to the detriment of the smaller rural places.
Working conditions in those smaller centres would be much better. The working men and women would not have to travel up to an hour, or more, to go to and from their work. They would have that extra time to spend with their families, most likely in their gardens at home. Walking on their way to work they would know and be able to say "hello" to everyone they met. They would be able to live much cheaper. They would not be holed up in a crowded apartment that makes unnatural living conditions. They would be able to raise their kiddies as God meant them to be raised. Kiddies are not even welcome in most apartments by landlords today. Conditions in large centres are working toward

The Address-Mr. Drope
holding down our natural increase in population. Natural increase beats any type of immigration that any country can think of. From the point of view of raising a family, the large congested city stinks. There is not even grass on the school playgrounds. Even our undertakers today furnish synthetic grass for our dead. Can we not supply a little of the natural grass for our children?
We have had much labour unrest in Canada, and probably will have more. Working conditions in smaller centres do not supply the same incentive to labour to go on strike as that given in the larger centres. In the smaller centre, each worker is not considered a cog in the wheel of industry, but is considered a wheel in the machinery that keeps industry running. I would suggest that any government would do well to find ways ana means to encourage decentralization.
Before I finish, I wish to make a few remarks on what I think is an important subject, which is health. We must give better health services to rural municipalities; not because we of rural municipalities wish to be pampered; but because it will be to our nation's benefit to give that better service. For the past five years our rural infant mortality rate has been from fifty-five to sixty per 1,000 live births, compared with thirty to forty-two per 1,000 live births in our urban areas. Really to bring home what these figures mean, I must say that we in Canada were greatly concerned over the loss of 41,000 of our youth in the six years of war; but in the same period of time, Canada has lost 130,000 infants in their first six months of life. Our infant mortality in Canada is nineteen per cent higher than in the United States. Are we as a nation not as hardy as the United States? Are we as a nation not as capable of giving our youth a chance to live?
There is a book entitled, "Canadian Mother and Child", edited by Ernest Couture, M.D., and published by the authority of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It has been my privilege to mail a copy of this book to hundreds of mothers in my riding of Bruce, and in all cases those copies are greatly appreciated. Our youth is the greatest asset that Canada has today, so let us give them the service they deserve.

speechtext:
In rising to take part in the debate, I should like to offer my congratulations to the four new members who were elected since the last session. Many subjects have been discussed in this debate, but very little has been said about our basic industry, which I am sure we all agree is agriculture. The constituency of
Northumberland, which I have the honour to represent, is situated in central Ontario east of the city of Toronto, bounded on the south by lake Ontario and on the north by Rice lake and Trent river. It is a great agricultural county dotted with many splendid towns, villages and tourist resorts that attract visitors from many other parts of the United States as well as from other parts of Canada. The waters of Rice lake and Trent river teem with fish of many varieties. We have also one of the best skiing runs in Ontario, situated on No. 45 highway eight miles north of the town of Cobourg.
Dairying is carried on extensively in this county. I wish to say something about the butter and cheese situation as it affects our county and nearly all parts of Canada. The Canadian people are great consumers of dairy products when they can get them. What do we find in the matter of butter? We have been rationed and controlled until we now find the government importing large quantities of New Zealand butter. The controlled prices of butter have been so low that farmers have been driven out of producing churning cream. The dairy farmers have been working long hours in milking cows and have not been compensated for the time they have put in. I am satisfied that our dairy farmers, if given a reasonable price, can produce all the dairy products that we require in this country. The cost of living index is being held at the expense of the farmers of Canada. This situation must be corrected; after all, our nation cannot exist without food and our food must first come from the farms.
Much has been said about keeping good times in this country. My opinion is that, if the agricultural industry is prosperous, it will provide the best market for the manufactured goods of our towns and cities. I was interested in hearing the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) tonight telling us something about the lumber industry and what the controls that are being kept on meant to the people of Canada. Apparently he forgot to say that the administration of those controls cost the tax payers of Canada considerable money. Many articles have advanced in price even with controls. Higher prices across the line in the United States are bound to affect this country. Price control tends to reduce competition and thus tends to remove the stimulus of increasing efficiency and service to the consumer. We have a great country here. A great many of our returned men are coming back and taking their places in all walks of life. I am just wondering how the returned soldier is going to make out with these houses which have cost so much, and about whose poor construe-

tion we have heard so much. I hate to see the young soldier saddled with the high price which these houses have cost. I am quite satisfied that, if they had been built under free enterprise, we would have had a better job done and would have had more houses.
